a8b88bab52ba8e4e: SEPANG: Reigning MotoGP champion and current leader Marc Marquez admitted he has a fight on his hands to keep Aprilia's Jorge Martin and Marco Bezzecchi at bay this weekend in Malaysia.

"I try to give 100% in every race, every session. We will also try to understand if we can fight with both Aprilia factory riders. We did an incredible fight (Australian MotoGP), and most important for us is that we finished with 12 points," said the Spaniard.
The 33-year-old Marquez seized the world championship lead after the Ducati star won last weekend's sprint race at Phillip Island.

That victory earned him 365 points, putting him 10 clear of his injured compatriot Martin, who suffered a broken wrist in that sprint duel after a nasty crash, having been involved in a thrilling battle against Marquez.
Marquez could have amassed an even bigger lead had Sunday's main race in Australia not been called off by bad weather.
As it stands, Martin will participate in Friday's first practice session to assess if he can compete in Sepang over the weekend.
Marquez is happy to see Martin racing.
"If Martin is on the racetrack, he will be fast," he said.
Italian Bezzecchi lies 50 points adrift of Marquez in the standings and is aware the challenge is a tough one.

"It's clear that if I want to try to stay in the fight, I have to try to not lose many points. It won’t be easy because everyone is super quick. I have to be competitive and try to fight for those positions," he said.
Unpredictable conditions at the Sepang circuit will be a test for the riders.
Torrential rain and suffocating humidity are expected to be prevalent throughout the race weekend.
After Malaysia, there are only three weekends left in the season.
a4cded515f47461a: HSINCHU: The Taiwan Semiconductor Industry Association (TSIA) said on Thursday it supports the government’s efforts to assess the possible restart of the country's nuclear power plants, citing the need for a stable and sufficient electricity supply to support the chip industry.

TSIA Chairman Cliff Hou, who is also a senior vice-president at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC), the world's largest contract chipmaker, said at the association’s annual convention that the industry had repeatedly called on the government to ensure a reliable power supply.
"A stable and sufficient electricity supply is crucial to the semiconductor industry," Hou said.

Hou said the association’s board agreed to formally support the government’s plans to evaluate the restart of nuclear power plants, provided the process complied with regulations and met safety requirements.
The TSIA’s members include major Taiwanese chipmakers like TSMC, United Microelectronics Corp (UMC), Vanguard International Semiconductor and PSMC.

Taiwanese president Lai Ching-te said in an interview earlier this month that his government would not rule out any form of energy, including nuclear power, as long as safety, nuclear waste disposal and public consensus requirements were met
“My position is very clear. We should not rule out any form of energy based on ideology,” Lai said.
Taiwan closed its last nuclear power plant in May last year as the government shifts to renewables and liquefied natural gas.
Taiwan’s main opposition party, the Kuomintang, wants Taiwan to bring back nuclear power.

697824f502d27faf: A hulking gray giant rises from the desert. Inside, engineers create the force behind our phones and computers and appliances, our streaming services and search engines and chatbots and vibe-coded apps and websites. The complex is simultaneously massive and squat, dwarfed by the mountains that surround it, and it is endless. I drive past one building, and then another, and then the ground opens up where construction crews have dug up the earth so a third building can rise. There is a parking lot, and then another, and then another. There is an empty lot on the other side of the street, full of cars and the occasional food truck to feed the thousands of laborers who are busy transforming this expanse of desert into an industrial park. There is dust, so much of it, choking the air.

I stand before the savior of Arizona’s economy. Like all great deities, it demands sacrifice. In the desert, nothing is more precious than water, and water is what must be given — nearly 5 million gallons a day, every day, sourced from Phoenix’s municipal supply. The offering has been well worth it.

All of this is the fruit of the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world’s leading producer of microchips. Its Arizona operation is the result of a pre-pandemic gamble Phoenix made to revive its sluggish economy, which never quite rebounded from the Great Recession. Now TSMC’s foundry looms over the city’s outskirts.

TSMC is a success story, one that some local leaders may have hoped to repeat with hyperscale data center developments. The progression may have seemed natural: The Grand Canyon State is not only home to the largest chip factory this side of the Pacific but also 172 data centers, neither of which faced much pushback. But the newer, larger developments being proposed from Phoenix to Tucson demand more of everything — more water, more power, more land — than Arizonans are willing to give. Where TSMC was welcomed with open arms and the first wave of data centers was largely ignored, new developments are facing mass backlash in Arizona, where a grassroots, surprisingly bipartisan coalition of residents has united against data centers.
Now the state has a sixth C, Arizona native Christine Mackay tells me. “Chips.”

In reporting this story, I spoke to local activists and economic developers, elected officials and their angry constituents. I sat in on city council meetings where people lined up by the dozens to speak up against data center projects, and in cozy suburban homes where tight-knit groups of former strangers told me about the struggle that brought them together. I pored over maps of Arizona’s dry, cracked landscape with laypeople who, over the past two years, have made themselves experts on zoning and land use and water consumption so they can understand the beast they’re trying to fight. The locals on both sides of this debate claim to want the same thing: a better, more prosperous Arizona. Their visions for achieving it, however, are completely at odds.

In Arizona and elsewhere, data center developers have tried to win over locals by making enticing promises about the jobs, tax revenue, and infrastructure they’ll bring with them. All they ask for in exchange is water — and, they swear, not nearly as much of it as you’d expect. Some hyperscale data centers, like Google’s facility in The Dalles, Oregon, use about 1.5 million gallons a day, about one-third of what TSMC’s Arizona complex consumes in the same timeframe. Those reassurances, however, aren’t enough to assuage Arizonans, who now have to contend with the fact that the state will soon lose access to nearly 30 percent of the water it receives from the Colorado River.

Even now, as people across the country sour on AI and fight against data centers in their communities, TSMC’s Arizona operation hums along without significant opposition. And yet it’s impossible to make sense of why Arizonans are so opposed to new data center development without first understanding why they eagerly welcomed TSMC, even though both industries must contend with the issue that has plagued Arizona since its founding: There isn’t enough water.

For as long as anyone could remember, business in Arizona revolved around the storied “five C’s”: cattle, copper, cotton, citrus, and climate, a catchall for the region’s mild, salubrious winters, which locals say often more than make up for the sweltering summers.
Now the state has a sixth C, Arizona native Christine Mackay tells me. “Chips.”

The TSMC development is, in a sense, Mackay’s doing. As the head of Phoenix’s economic development office, she spearheaded the effort that brought the Taiwanese giant to the Sonoran Desert. In 2020, while the global economy was all but shut down, TSMC made an announcement. The same forces that brought the world to a standstill had created even more demand for TSMC’s products, and in response, TSMC would be opening an advanced semiconductor foundry — a “fab,” in industry jargon — in Phoenix. Initially, TSMC predicted that it would pour $12 billion into Arizona’s economy by 2029. Since then, TSMC’s projected expenditure in the state has ballooned to $265 billion, what the company touts as the largest foreign direct investment in US history.

TSMC just put the finishing touches on its second fab in a formerly desolate swath of north Phoenix, with a third under construction and plans for several more underway. This buildout has been more than a decade in the making. TSMC started shopping around for a US location in 2016. That year, Mackay said, the company put out a request for proposals through a codename. No one won.

“We aren’t a group that takes no for an answer,” Mackay said proudly. Her office asked TSMC executives what they thought Arizona was missing, and then spent the next three years addressing their concerns. In 2019, Phoenix sent a delegation to Taiwan to share a new development plan for a science and technology park, the nucleus of which would be a factory, ideally one of TSMC’s fabs. “They agreed they needed to come back and take another look at Phoenix,” Mackay told me. Her team showed them two locations: Laveen, Arizona, a suburb southwest of Phoenix, and, just north of the city, an undeveloped area roughly the size of Manhattan called Biscuit Flats, so named, Mackay told me, because “it’s as round and flat as a biscuit.”
“That very day,” she recalled, “they said, ‘This could work.’”

What followed was a flurry of development unlike anything the state has ever seen. TSMC has brought more than 3,500 jobs to the state, and an entire economy has sprung up to support the company’s Arizona operation. Much like in Taiwan — where the company accounts for nearly one-tenth of Taiwan’s gross domestic product — TSMC has become, if not the center of the universe, then at least a galaxy unto itself. The company controls an estimated 70 percent of the global chip market, and its contracts with Apple and Nvidia alone make up more than one-third of its annual revenue. (Apple and Nvidia design their own chips, but they don’t produce them. The complex manufacturing process is instead largely outsourced to TSMC.)

TSMC has changed swaths of Phoenix — its landscape, its industries — and it has brought with it jobs and prosperity. Locals fear that the new hyperscale data center developments will do the former but not the latter, consuming resources while contributing little to the community. Mackay, who has worked as an economic developer for over 30 years, didn’t experience significant pushback when she helped court data center developments in the past. “The first 10 data centers I did look like pretty little office buildings,” she said.

The new developments being proposed are neither pretty nor little. Where earlier data centers were inconspicuous, the hyperscale facilities developers want to build in Arizona — often on rural farm or desert land — are both massive and incongruous. Despite the state’s recently acquired reputation for sprawl, there are still plenty of places where, in the quiet desert stillness, you can sometimes hear a pack of coyotes howl in the middle of the night. There are dark-sky corridors and wild animals, ghost towns and saguaro forests. All of this, some locals say, could be sacrificed for the benefit of an industry that also poses an existential threat to humanity. There are ethical questions and environmental ones, debates over zoning and taxes and, most of all, over water. Yet the cities and the outlying suburbs keep growing, spreading in all directions until they’re constrained by geography or bureaucracy or Indigenous sovereignty. And industry, somehow, keeps arriving, thirstier than ever.

Year-round but especially in the summers, Arizonans tailor their routines to the elements. Drivers are careful not to get stuck in dust storms or monsoons. Joggers avoid going out in late mornings and early afternoons, when the heat is at its most intense. And on August 1st, at the peak of monsoon season, the No Desert Data Center Coalition’s protest began in the early evening, when the sun’s punishing rays were starting to give way to a muted desert sunset.

About a dozen people showed up to the rally on the outskirts of Tucson, in front of the 290-acre site where Beale Infrastructure is building a 600-megawatt data center. Every few minutes, Vivek Bharathan, one of the organizers, reminded the protesters to stay hydrated. Children sprayed each other with water guns and dutifully accepted drinks from their parents. Mayra Duron, one of the attendees, brought a cooler of agua de jamaica to share with the group. The magenta beverage, she said, was full of electrolytes. Water — the lack of it, the need for it, the amount required to build a massive data center in the middle of the desert — was top of mind. A hand-painted banner expressed the overarching sentiment: BEALE’S DATA CENTER WILL SUCK US DRY.

“If you feel the heat, please head home,” Bharathan told the small crowd. “It is a hot day, and if they succeed in building a data center here, it’ll be even hotter. We know these things create heat islands that can affect the surrounding area by over 10 degrees Fahrenheit.” Duron, a local macrame artist who incorporates cactus spines into her weaving, said she worried about how rising temperatures would affect the region’s saguaros. “In Phoenix, it’s hyper-industrialized,” she said, “and they’ve seen saguaros die left and right.”

Cars honked in support. Some drivers pumped their fists out their windows as they sped by. Arizonans weren’t riled up about AI in 2019, when the TSMC project was announced, nor did they notice or care much about the previous data centers that were quietly built throughout the state. Things have changed. Tucson, it appears, is united in its opposition to the data center complex dubbed Project Blue. But the buildings are going up anyway.
“We take it as normal because it’s been that way for so long. But it isn’t normal. It’s a catastrophe.”

Information about Project Blue began slowly trickling out in the spring of 2025. First came the name, and some clues: The development, whatever it was, would be on a county-owned plot of land; it would create 3,000 temporary construction jobs and 200 well-paying positions down the road; it would generate $152 million in tax revenue over the next decade; it would be big, and it would be thirsty, and new water lines would be built to keep it satiated. That was all anyone in the know would say, because the county government, which owned the land, signed a nondisclosure agreement with the would-be developer.

The news came out in a mundane, bureaucratic way, as information about prospective land sales in midsize cities often does. In June 2025, Jan Lesher, the Pima County administrator, submitted a 44-page memo to the Board of Supervisors. The words “data center” did not appear until the fourth page. This data center would provide an “unprecedented” $3.6 billion opportunity for Tucson and for the county. There were other details, and there was flattery, and there were promises. Project Blue would use “100% renewable water resources.” Its developer, Beale Infrastructure, would build critical infrastructure at its own expense, including an 18-mile pipe extension and an aquifer recharge facility.

“The boost it could provide to our local economy may well be transformative,” Rex Scott, one of five members of the County Board of Supervisors, said at the time. His colleagues were split. They voted 3-2 to rezone the 290-acre tract, and voted again to sell it to Beale for around $20 million. But it wasn’t a guarantee yet. One of the terms of the deal required Tucson to annex the land and approve the sale, since the city would be on the hook for the land’s water service.

The honeymoon, if there even was one, didn’t last. Just hours after the board’s vote, Tucson Electric Power announced it was looking into a rate hike that would increase customers’ bills by an average of 14 percent. The utility claimed the decision was unrelated to the forthcoming data center. Even still, one of the commissioners who voted to rezone the land and sell it to Beale officially asked to reconsider the rezoning.

Perhaps it was the fact that Tucsonans learned of the data center and the rate hike in such quick succession, coupled with the inescapable news of data centers raising locals’ utility bills, that catalyzed their mass opposition. Maybe it was the Arizona Mirror’s report that Project Blue, combined with another proposed data center, would not only be TEP’s biggest customer but also consume more than four golf courses’ worth of water each year. The fact that Amazon Web Services was reportedly the end client — and that county officials had been discussing the project since 2023, and, according to public records obtained by Arizona Luminaria, signed NDAs prohibiting them from naming the companies involved — certainly didn’t help. Whatever the reason, Beale executives probably weren’t prepared for just how angry the public would be.

Around 200 people showed up to a public information meeting Beale hosted in the auditorium of a local high school in July 2025. Most of them were furious about the data center, or they were worried, or they were scared. Tensions were even higher at the follow-up meeting held at the Tucson Convention Center. Over a thousand people showed up. The boos started before Beale’s representatives got through their introductions, and they continued throughout the night.

Keri Silvyn, one of the attorneys representing Beale, tried to warm up the crowd. “We all have cellphones, we have computers, a number of us have multiple of those in our households,” she said. “Many of the various signs that I’ve seen have QR codes, that if you click on, will take you through a data center in order to get to different sites. The internet is housed in data centers. That’s what they are.” Beale’s team explained that they selected the site because it was far from residential areas, and then they reiterated the now familiar pitch data center developers make to wary communities. Beale said it would pay for a pipeline, and once the pipeline was built the data center would run on reclaimed water. (Until then, however, it would rely on potable water.) The company would pay to clean up contaminated water. It would inject any extra water into local aquifers, eventually making the whole thing “water-positive.” None of this mollified the thousand or so people in the audience, who booed every few minutes.

To no one’s surprise, the opposition mostly came down to water. Locals worried that if the data center came to town, the resource, already so scarce and so precious, would vanish. They cited the fact that Arizona would likely lose more of its Colorado River allotment. They conjured images of even hotter, drier summers.
“Can you guarantee us water for future generations?”

When it was her turn to speak, Melanie Cooley, an education specialist at the Watershed Management Group, a local habitat restoration nonprofit, conjured up a past familiar to few Tucsonans. “Where we are sitting right now was a forest 125 years ago that adjoined a flowing river that flowed year-round,” she said. “There are people alive today who grew up swimming in the Santa Cruz River.”

Average temperatures in Tucson are now 11 degrees Fahrenheit higher than they were a century ago, Cooley said. About six degrees of that rise can be attributed to global warming. The other five, Cooley explained, are because of changes in the local ecosystem, including the felling of forests and the drying up of rivers like the Santa Cruz. “What we see today when we drive across that river that looks like a big, dry ditch, we take it as normal because it’s been that way for so long. But it isn’t normal. It’s a catastrophe. It’s a catastrophe that was brought on by overpumping of our groundwater and bad development decisions, and Project Blue is another bad development decision.”

Another speaker compared Project Blue to industrial projects of decades past. “This is like déjà vu for me,” he said, listing off economic development projects that were supposed to turn things around for the city: Raytheon; Hughes, the military contractor that preceded it; the Air National Guard. “What did they do? They contaminated our water. To this day, we’re having to deal with that.” Tucsonans had gone to great lengths to conserve their water. “We took our landscaping out, we took our swimming pools out.” He waved over a relative who was holding an infant in a sling. “Can you guarantee us water for future generations?” he asked the Beale representatives. “Can you guarantee water for her generation, my kids’ generation, my grandkids’ generation, and this little baby’s generation?”

Two days after this contentious hearing, a unanimous vote by the Tucson City Council shut down the annexation of the land. At a subsequent meeting, the city adopted new rules for data centers and other large water users. Residents were relieved, but not for long. Three weeks after the city stopped the annexation, effectively killing the development, local reporters confirmed that Beale was moving forward with the data center anyway. County officials and Beale representatives had previously said that the deal was contingent on Tucson’s annexation of the land. Suddenly that was no longer an issue. (Beale declined to comment on why annexation was no longer necessary for the deal.)

Over time, there were other adjustments to the plan: The data center would no longer be water-cooled and would instead rely on closed-loop air cooling. If the shift was intended to win over Beale’s critics, it didn’t work. Members of the No Desert Data Center Coalition claim that air-cooled facilities use more electricity, and, since power plants also use water to cool their systems, air-cooled data centers may actually be more water-intensive, just indirectly, an allegation Beale denies. “The use of air-cooled technology for this project does not increase overall energy use; while the energy allocation is different, the energy use is the same,” Beale spokesperson Tony Burkart, the Beale spokesperson, told The Verge. (Energy generation does require water, though there’s little data on just how much water Arizona’s power plants consume.) The change also cost Beale a tenant: Amazon reportedly pulled out of the project, saying an air-cooled facility wouldn’t meet its needs. Beale declined to disclose whether it has since found a new tenant for Project Blue. “It’s up to our tenants when they choose to announce their investment in a project,” Burkart said.
ecd0e51d946a224e: PETALING JAYA: MCA has been allocated one more seat to contest in the Nov 14 Melaka state election, with Barisan Nasional to vie for 22 seats in total instead of 21 as announced previously.

MCA president Wee Ka Siong said the party will also contest the Chinese-majority seat of Bandar Hilir following the latest round of discussions between BN and Perikatan Nasional, which have formed an alliance for the Melaka polls.
He said the party will field Jasmine Lok, 38, a Melaka city councillor, to vie for the DAP stronghold.
"At 4pm, BN chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi handed the candidate her letter of appointment (surat watikah)," Wee said at a press conference in Parliament.
Wee said this meant PN will only contest six seats in the state election.
"PN's top leadership has stated their readiness to let MCA contest, because this is a seat that we have always contested.

"MCA is familiar to voters in the area, and we have a local councillor serving there. Also, Bandar Hilir falls under the Kota Melaka parliamentary constituency, which is also another traditional seat of MCA's," he said.
This will be Lok's first time running for election. She is also the Melaka MCA information chief and has served as a Melaka city local councillor since 2022.
Chinese voters make up about 73% of the electorate in the Bandar Hilir constituency, established in 1974. DAP won the seat first, before MCA held it from 1982 to 1995.
Since then, DAP has kept a firm grip on Bandar Hilir, winning with a 7,778-vote majority in the 2021 polls.
Last week, Wee led an MCA walkout as BN unveiled its candidates for the state polls, saying the Chinese-based component was not consulted about the seat allocation.
After discussions with Zahid and other BN leaders yesterday, Wee later said MCA agreed to contest just the two seats.
73686718715a7fd8: Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.

Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century.

A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs, and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding.

None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. Many of them don’t incorporate any. That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries.

A separate analysis published in One Earth in March, which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed. It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds.

Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects. Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group.

At least some of this is starting to happen. Spark kick-started an initiative, called the Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project, through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power. Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029. That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds.

But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution. And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue.

So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control. Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in a recent feature story). In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has backed lab research on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetlands to counteract fast-rising methane emissions.

Several startups are also exploring possibilities. They’re looking into suppressing the lightning strikes that are igniting more and more fires in high latitudes, placing synthetic mats above permafrost to prevent it from melting, and deploying autonomous drones to quickly suppress potentially high-emissions fires before they burn out of control.

Investigating all these ideas is worthwhile. But researchers are only in the earliest stages of figuring out how big a dent in emissions any such efforts could achieve across sprawling global ecosystems undergoing massive transformations.
The surest path to reducing the effect of warming-driven warming remains the one we’ve known all along: breaking society’s addiction to fossil fuels.
This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.

That investigation found Instagram accounts with hundreds of thousands of followers and millions of views uploaded videos filmed with Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses, where men entered massage parlors across the country and solicited the workers for sex work. The full letter is here.

“Meta’s own disclosures confirm that imagery processed through its glasses’ visual AI features may be retained and used to train AI systems, including with the assistance of human reviewers,” the letter says. “Using intimate imagery for AI development is itself an invasion of privacy when the people depicted have not consented to that use, as is inherently the case for most bystanders captured by Meta’s glasses. Retaining that material for AI development, thereby extending the period during which it can be accessed, disclosed, or misused, exploits people’s highly sensitive information for Meta’s commercial benefit.”
Researchers Show How Meta's 'Pervert Glasses' Are Used to Harass Women
A new study shows how pickup artist influencers use smart glasses to create content, and the connection between covert recording and harm.

Research published in August revealed how Meta’s platforms encourage an ecosystem of abusive, harassing content from pickup artists and influencers who use Meta’s smart glasses to capture interactions with people minding their own business in public or at their workplaces, who might not even know they’re being filmed. In a January report by the BBC, a woman who was recorded with the glasses said she was “bombarded” with phone calls because her phone number was posted with the video, and men who had seen the video stalked her at work.

Earlier this year, more than 70 people sued Meta, claiming that their intimate images and videos were exposed to workers hired by the company to label the data for AI. In March, Swedish journalists reported that Kenyan data labelers were viewing and annotating uncensored footage from Meta’s smart glasses, including sexual and violent content; Meta ended its contract with those workers less than two months later. These are labor conditions that groups like the Data Labelers Association in Kenya are fighting back against, and for the people whose images are in the videos and photos, it’s an obvious violation of their privacy. People have also been modding these glasses to disable the light that indicates they’re recording for years

Meta has played dumb about the difference between AI glasses you wear on your face and an iPhone for a long time. Now, these senators want the tech giant to answer for themselves. In the letter, Wyden and Markey demand answers about what safeguards, if any, Meta has in place to prevent the nonconsensual “capture, disclosure, or processing of sensitive and intimate imagery,” whether Meta specifically evaluated the potential for its glasses “to facilitate voyeurism, nonconsensual intimate image capture, or similar privacy invasions,” what imagery it uses for AI training, and whether people can request their biometric and other data captured by its glasses be deleted, along with several more questions about the glasses’ safety and design.

“The reported disclosure of intimate footage to contractors for the purpose of AI training is particularly disturbing. Human review to fulfill a service knowingly requested by the person depicted is one thing; exposing unsuspecting individuals’ intimate moments to strangers for AI training is quite another,” Wyden and Markey wrote. “The individuals whose naked bodies, sexual activity, and other private moments have reportedly been captured by Meta glasses did not knowingly agree to having those images shared with strangers, much less for the purpose of improving Meta’s commercial AI systems. That disclosure and processing is an invasion of privacy, regardless of whether the footage is subsequently published or misused.”

Do you know anything else about harassment and Meta's smart glasses? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at sam.404. Otherwise, send me an email at sam@404media.co.

In the last few weeks, Meta has come under fire for quietly changing its privacy policies for business accounts and granting itself permission to scrape user’s content and connected websites to develop its AI products.

Meta has been pushing its smart glasses over the years with ads featuring A-list celebrities, including Chris Pratt, Chris Hemsworth, and Kris Jenner (all three in a 2025 Superbowl ad), Doja Cat, Jennie Kim from K-pop group BLACKPINK, and most recently, Kylie Jenner. Guerrilla ad makers have countered with their own anti-AI glasses ads around the world, and people have started calling the smart glasses "pervert glasses" in response to these widespread invasions of privacy they've come to represent. In August, Meta filed a patent to add facial recognition and highlight reel features to its smart glasses.

e79c67180a76ef76: KUALA LUMPUR: The Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) has ordered former Yayasan Bank Rakyat chairman Datuk Seri Nazir Hussin Akhtar Hussin and his elder brother, Datuk Mubarak Hussain Akhtar Husin, to declare their assets.
Both men were issued asset declaration notices on Oct 20, with Nazir understood to have received his at the MACC headquarters in Putrajaya.
Mubarak was served at his residence.
MACC chief commissioner Datuk Seri Abd Halim Aman confirmed that both men had received and accepted the notices issued under Section 36 of the MACC Act.
He told the New Straits Times that they had 30 days to declare their assets, with a possible 30-day extension upon request.
Under Section 36, MACC may require individuals to furnish information on their assets, including movable and immovable property, financial holdings and other interests.
Investigators may also seek explanations on the sources of funds used to acquire assets to determine whether their wealth is consistent with known sources of income.
Earlier this month, Nazir spent about two hours at the MACC headquarters in connection with the asset declaration notice.
He later said his legal team had filed an injunction application at the Kuala Lumpur High Court to challenge the notice and prevent MACC from enforcing it.
Nazir said he could still be arrested despite the pending application and urged the commission to respect the legal process.
On Oct 1, MACC arrested Nazir and Mubarak in connection with an investigation into alleged collusion and abuse of power involving an investment of about RM10 million.

Initial investigations found that the two allegedly colluded with an officer of an education-based foundation to approve the investment in a company owned by the elder brother of one of the suspects in late 2020.
MACC also seized 15 luxury cars, 12 high-powered motorcycles, five luxury watches, three bracelets and about RM30,000 in cash.
4ba50ca79afa8cda: SEPANG, Oct 29 — Aprilia Racing’s Jorge Martin could add another dimension to the 2026 Malaysian Motorcycle Grand Prix (MotoGP) as championship leader Marc Marquez and third-placed Marco Bezzecchi welcome the Spaniard’s return to action at the Sepang International Circuit (SIC).
Martin, who fractured his right wrist in a crash during a Sprint battle with title rival Marquez at Phillip Island last Saturday, has been declared fit to participate in Friday’s practice session.
Marquez said he was pleased to see Martin back on the track, adding that riders would naturally try to compete whenever possible.

“Yeah, first of all, happy to see Martin on track because, as we know, a rider will try. But especially with the medical protocol that we have introduced in recent years, if they are fit, it means that it is safe.
“So, yeah, if Martin is on the racetrack, he will be fast,” he said at a press conference here today.
Meanwhile, Bezzecchi also welcomed Martin’s return, saying he would have made the same decision if he were in a similar situation.
“Yeah, I agree with Marc. First of all, happy to see him. Obviously, I think we have both been in a similar situation, so for sure, in the same situation, we would have tried.
“So, it’s good to have him here. Hopefully, he will feel good,” he said.
Marquez leads the championship standings with 365 points (pts), just 10 ahead of Martin on 355pts, while Bezzecchi sits third overall with 315pts.

34781f222dc7f5db: JAKARTA: Pandu Sjahrir, the prominent Indonesian wealth fund executive who has publicly supported MSCI Inc.’s scrutiny of the nation’s stock market, is the co-owner of a brokerage sanctioned in connection with a stock-market manipulation probe.
Pandu, who as chief investment officer of Danantara has become a key liaison with global money managers, indirectly owns a 27.5% stake in PT Supra Sekuritas Indonesia, according to company records.

People with knowledge of the matter, who asked not to be identified discussing sensitive information, said Supra Sekuritas was the company referred to as “SS” by Indonesia’s Financial Services Authority this month when it announced sanctions against more than a dozen entities for violating regulations in cases related to market manipulation.

The statement, which only listed the firms by their initials, came in the wake of MSCI’s surprise threat to downgrade the country to standalone status — a more severe punishment than previously considered.

The previously unreported revelation risks complicating Indonesia’s efforts to regain New York-based MSCI’s confidence and prevent billions of dollars in capital outflows. The nation’s benchmark stock index has dropped around 10% since the index provider’s warning on Oct 15, the worst performance in Asia.

MSCI has repeatedly raised concerns about opaque ownership and the potential for coordinated trading in one of Southeast Asia’s biggest equity markets, while pressing authorities to strengthen regulation, surveillance and enforcement.
As a top executive at Danantara, which reports to President Prabowo Subianto, Pandu has pitched the country to investors at global forums in places like Washington, Davos and Tokyo.

“Pandu has increasingly become the face of Indonesia to the international investment community,” said Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara, executive director of the Center of Economic and Law Studies, a Jakarta-based think tank.
A spokesperson for Pandu confirmed in a statement that he’s a minority shareholder of Supra Sekuritas in his personal capacity, noting that the investment is passive.

Pandu has never served on the company’s “board of directors, board of commissioners, or management, and has had no role in its daily operations, trading activities or compliance decisions,” the spokesperson said. “His ownership should not be confused with responsibility for the company’s actions.”

Pandu fully respects the FSA and “supports strong and fair enforcement of capital market regulations,” the spokesperson said, adding that he “remains committed to supporting transparency, good governance and investor confidence in Indonesia’s capital markets.”
In recent months, MSCI has privately signaled to Indonesian officials, including Pandu, that the market’s problems have not been fixed, according to people familiar with the matter.

Pandu has publicly supported MSCI’s scrutiny, describing its warning as a much needed wake-up call to improve the Indonesian stock market’s liquidity and transparency. The alumni of Stanford Graduate School of Business had estimated a downgrade to frontier-market status alone could trigger US$25 billion to US$50 billion in outflows.

Pandu met with MSCI Chief Executive Henry Fernandez in late September in New York and asked for recommendations on what Indonesia could do to avoid a reclassification, people familiar with that gathering said. On Oct. 13, Pandu participated in a Danantara-organized event on the sidelines of IMF meetings in Bangkok that MSCI also attended.

The announcement of fines earlier this month was part of the biggest series of financial penalties ever laid out by the FSA — a sweeping response to MSCI’s downgrade threat. The Indonesian regulator said on Monday that it will name sanctioned entities after an appeals period, but didn’t provide a timeline.

Pandu owns 99.99% of PT Asha Artha Sehati, which in turn holds a 27.5% stake in Supra Sekuritas, according to Bloomberg calculations of shareholding shown in company registration records. The brokerage, formerly known as Supra Securinvest, has been a trader of shares in Indonesian coal miner PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa, one of the companies at the heart of the recent regulatory sanctions.

His broader business career spans energy and private capital. Pandu spent 15 years helping run PT TBS Energi Utama, a listed group rooted in coal mining that has expanded into waste management, renewable energy and electric mobility. He directly held about 0.6% of its shares at the end of April.

Pandu was also a managing partner at Indies Capital and a founding partner of AC Ventures, which have reported managing more than US$1 billion and US$500 million, respectively. Those figures reflect capital managed for investors, rather than Pandu’s personal assets.
MSCI has said it will make a decision on Indonesia’s market status by the end of June 2027.

ff6d132f5c34c831: KUALA LUMPUR: Bersatu president Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin said the confidence and supply agreement (CSA) signed with the government had no connection to any electoral pact with Pakatan Harapan (PH) in the Melaka election.
Asked by reporters whether Bersatu would form an electoral pact with PH in Melaka, he said: "That's another question. Today, this has no connection here."

He was speaking after signing the agreement at Parliament here with several other Bersatu members of Parliament, including Datuk Seri Radzi Jidin (Putrajaya), Datuk Ali Biju (Saratok), Datuk Mohd Suhaimi Abdullah (Langkawi), Mohd Nazri Abu Hassan (Merbok) and Azman Nasrudin (Padang Serai).
Asked whether the CSA would also apply to a similar agreement being sought between Bersatu and the PH-led Selangor government, he gave a similar answer.
"That's another question. This is between the federal government - the prime minister - and the members of Parliament representing my party and other parties," he said.
Those spotted at the signing also included Opposition Leader Datuk Seri Hamzah Zainudin and Muar MP Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman.

Earlier, the government and several opposition MPs signed the agreement. Deputy Prime Ministers Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi and Datuk Seri Fadillah Yusof, as well as Datuk Seri Azalina Othman Said and Tengku Datuk Seri Zafrul Abdul Aziz, were also present.

Under the agreement, the MPs pledged to support the 2027 Budget and institutional reforms, including limiting the prime minister's tenure to a maximum of two terms and separating the roles of the attorney-general and public prosecutor.
The government, meanwhile, agreed to provide opposition MPs with development allocations equal to those given to government MPs from today and to cover the Bumiputera agenda.

An online portal previously reported that Selangor Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Amirudin Shari had said a CSA would be signed with Bersatu before the Selangor Budget was tabled next month, subject to approval from PH's top leadership.
The Melaka state election will be held on Nov 14, with nomination on Oct 31.
1baa2db15b35ff81: SEPANG: An intense weekend of action awaits fans at the Petronas Grand Prix of Malaysia, which begins tomorrow, as the MotoGP title race heats up at Sepang.
With only 50 points separating the top three in the premier class, there will be little margin for error.

Jorge Martin (Aprilia Racing), who is 10 points adrift of championship leader Marc Marquez (Ducati Lenovo), has been cleared to take part in free practice one (FP1) tomorrow but will have to undergo another medical checkup after that.
Martin's participation at Sepang had been in doubt as he had crashed while duelling with Marquez during the sprint race at Phillip Island last week and fractured his wrist.
Marquez said he was pleased to see Martin, the 2024 world champion, at Sepang.
"First of all, I am happy to see Jorge on track. As we know, a rider will always try to race," said Marquez during a press conference here today.
"With all the medical protocols introduced over the last few years, if they (medical team) say he is fit, that means it is safe for him to race.
"If Jorge is on the racetrack, he will be fine."
Marco Bezzecchi, who is 50 points behind Marquez in third, said he would do the same if he was in Martin's situation.
Martin, who is Bezzecchi's teammate, opted not to return to Spain to receive treatment after the crash as he was keen to race at Sepang.
"I think we (with Marquez) have both been in a similar situation. For sure, we would have tried (to race)," said Bezzecchi during the same presser.
"It is good to have him here, hopefully he will be feeling good. If he feels good, for sure he will be fast."
Bezzecchi has downplayed his chances of chasing down Marquez in the championship race.
Ducati team manager Davide Tardozzi had last week said Bezzecchi has the potential to win all remaining races this season.
"I appreciate it, but not everything he said is true. 50 points is still 50 points," said Bezzecchi.
"In races anything can happen. I appreciate what they think about me but it is never easy. I am not complaining, I just want to give it my best."
Bezzecchi, who finished third overall in the championship last season, has never finished on the podium at Sepang before.
Marquez, despite being one of the greatest riders of all time, has only won two MotoGP races here (2014, 2018).
Martin won the sprint race and was second in the main race here in 2024. He was forced to sit out most of last season due to injury and did not race in Malaysia last year.

178eb837e279e69c: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 29 — Menara Tun Perak, the iconic Kuala Lumpur skyscraper formerly known as Menara Maybank, has reportedly been put up for sale after serving as the banking giant’s headquarters for nearly four decades.

According to a sponsored announcement published by property news website Mingtiandi, investors are being offered the opportunity to acquire either a partial or full interest in the building, although no asking price was disclosed.
Standing 244 metres tall along Jalan Tun Perak, the building was completed in 1988 and remains one of the capital’s most recognisable landmarks.
The proposed sale comes months after Maybank relocated its headquarters to Merdeka 118 on May 6, ending its longstanding use of the tower as its head office.
On July 28, Maybank announced that its new headquarters would be renamed Menara Merdeka Maybank, while its former headquarters would take the name Menara Tun Perak.
Property consultancy firms Knight Frank Malaysia and CBRE|WTW have reportedly been jointly appointed to advise on the proposed sale.
The building’s location near Chinatown, Central Market, Dataran Merdeka and several public transport stations is being promoted as a key attraction for potential investors.

According to the announcement, interested buyers could retain the property for commercial use, upgrade the existing building or explore converting it into a hotel, serviced accommodation or mixed-use development, subject to feasibility studies and regulatory approvals.
Knight Frank Malaysia head of capital markets James Buckley said properties of such prominence in Kuala Lumpur's historic commercial district were seldom offered to investors.
“Landmark assets of this nature, particularly those located within the city’s historic core, are rarely made available for investment,” he said.
CBRE|WTW director Marcus Yeo said the building's location and potential for alternative uses could appeal to investors amid the continued redevelopment of Kuala Lumpur's city centre.

f7a84fca07c10471: JAKARTA: Indonesian police are investigating 97 corporations, including 22 foreign-linked companies, over forest and land fire cases across the country, with 20 companies already named as suspects.

National Police Criminal Investigation Agency (Bareskrim) chief Comm Gen Asep Safrudin said 16 of the 20 corporate suspects were domestically invested companies, while the remaining four were foreign-invested.
"The number of corporate suspects may increase as our investigations continue," he said at a press conference in Pontianak, West Kalimantan, on Thursday, which was streamed live on social media.
Asep said the corporate suspects have designated management representatives for legal proceedings, with investigation papers to be submitted to public prosecutors before heading to court.
The companies are being investigated under Articles 98, 99, and 108 of the Environmental Protection and Management Law, which cover deliberate or negligent environmental offences and land burning.
The offences carry penalties of up to 15 years' imprisonment for individuals found liable and fines of up to 15 billion rupiah (RM3.36 million).
"We are proceeding against foreign-affiliated companies or those funded by overseas investment because the alleged offences occurred within the jurisdiction of the Republic of Indonesia," he said.

Asep said police have recommended the revocation of business licences of 23 corporations following findings that included repeated fires within concessions, fires originating on company land, inadequate firefighting facilities, and burned areas exceeding 500 hectares.

He said police had so far received 104 reports involving corporations, covering 29,168.78 hectares of burned land, including 33 reports in West Kalimantan, 20 in South Sumatra, 14 in Central Kalimantan, 13 in South Kalimantan, and seven in East Kalimantan.
For cases involving individuals, police have filed 287 reports covering 5,859.12 hectares of burned land, with 245 people named as suspects.
West Kalimantan recorded the highest number of police reports involving individuals, at 68, followed by Riau (59), Central Kalimantan (43), South Sumatra (42) and East Kalimantan (30).
Asep said that individual cases generally involved deliberate or negligent burning to clear land, with suspects investigated under environmental protection, plantation, and forestry laws.

d0fc80649cae12ab: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 29 — National triathlete Esther Joy Chen is eyeing an opportunity to compete in the marathon at the 2027 Kuala Lumpur SEA Games after emerging as Malaysia’s fastest female runner at the Standard Chartered Kuala Lumpur Marathon on October 4.

Esther, 22, clocked three hours, five minutes and 22 seconds (3:05:22) to win the Malaysian women’s category in her marathon debut, putting herself on the preliminary list of candidates for selection for the biennial Games.

She said the achievement had motivated her to continue improving her performance, particularly in terms of physical and mental preparation, as she pursued her dream of representing Malaysia on the international stage.

“In my mind, I am an optimistic person. I like setting high targets because I believe that whatever we set our minds to, we can achieve,” she said on Lensa Wanita on Siara Bernama Radio at Wisma Bernama here today.
On her preparations, Esther said she underwent specialised marathon training, with between one and three sessions a day depending on her training needs, each lasting between one and three hours.
She said nutrition during races also required attention, particularly the intake of energy gels and drinks, to help improve her performance.
“I think, in terms of performance, my race nutrition, especially energy gels and drinks, is still an area that needs improvement. Once I get that right, I believe I can go faster,” she said.

Esther, who began focusing more seriously on sports only last year, said the support of her partner and family had also played an important role in helping her get through difficult days during training.
She previously joined a wushu development programme in 2014 before quitting. She also had experience in gymnastics during her school days before turning her focus to triathlon.

Commenting on the challenges of triathlon, Esther said swimming was the most challenging discipline for her, as she had started swimming at the age of eight before stopping and resuming training at 18.

She hoped to continue addressing her weaknesses and building her self-confidence as she prepared to face greater challenges, including the opportunity to compete at the 2027 Kuala Lumpur SEA Games. — Bernama
ffb9fc4e0c140bb5: KOTA BARU: Violent threats from smugglers are part of life for border enforcement personnel.
Smugglers they encounter shout threats at them and occasionally fire shots at them using firearms and air guns.
A former member of a border enforcement unit who only wanted to be identified as Irwandi said he was once shot at with an air gun.
He said he had patrolled the border between Kelantan and Thailand from 2004 till 2022, during which time he had encountered smugglers on several occasions.
The 48-year-old said, during one such encounter, the smugglers fired air guns at his unit, though the shot missed him and his colleagues.
"There were times when we faced threats from smugglers. They would use air guns to intimidate us, and the situation could become dangerous, especially during patrols at night," he said.
Irwandi said smuggling activities along the border involved various contraband, including drugs, firearms and rice.
He said smugglers often operated between 2am and 3am, when most people were asleep, and took advantage of the quiet surroundings to move their goods across the river.
The shallow waters of Sungai Golok also made it easier for smugglers to cross, particularly during the dry season.
"They know the river very well. When the water level drops, crossing becomes much easier, allowing them to move their goods quickly to the other side," he said.
Irwandi said syndicates also had informers who alerted them whenever enforcement personnel were spotted conducting patrols.
He said such warnings made enforcement work more challenging, as smugglers could quickly change their routes or abandon their plans when they learnt of the presence of authorities.
He said tighter security measures and strict adherence to standard operating procedures were crucial whenever threats or attempts to obstruct enforcement operations occurred.

On Tuesday, the New Straits Times had reported that villagers along the Kelantan coast claim they have been threatened with firearms by members of human-smuggling syndicates to stop them from exposing illegal activities in their neighbourhoods.
They said the threats had heightened fear among coastal communities, where undocumented migrants were brought ashore almost nightly through rivers, jetties and secluded stretches of beach.
Meanwhile, marine policemen have been ordered to double their operations to curb human-trafficking activities along the Kelantan and Golok rivers as well as waters off Tumpat.

Marine police Region Three commander Assistant Commissioner Mohd Khairuddin Jamal said the directive to strengthen surveillance and enforcement had been issued to all, particularly those operating in Pengkalan Kubor, Tumpat.
He said the number of marine policemen on duty had also been increased in the effort to prevent syndicates from exploiting the country's waterways to smuggle migrants into Malaysia.
"In terms of assets and manpower, operations that were previously conducted twice a week must now be doubled, along with the number of personnel involved," he said when contacted.
Khairuddin said the operations would focus on identified hotspots and routes frequently used by syndicates to transport undocumented migrants.
However, he said the syndicates frequently changed their modus operandi to evade detection.

b42230a46e5328cb: PETALING JAYA: Prosiding jenayah terhadap tertuduh yang meninggal dunia sebelum perbicaraan perlu direkodkan sebagai dihentikan, bukannya dilepas atau dibebaskan, putus Mahkamah Tinggi di Johor Bahru.

348463c3f2b4c4b9: JAKARTA: Indonesian police are investigating 97 corporations, including 22 foreign-linked companies, over forest and land fire cases across the country, with 20 companies already named as suspects.

National Police Criminal Investigation Agency (Bareskrim) chief comm gen Asep Safrudin said 16 of the 20 corporate suspects were domestically invested companies, while the remaining four were foreign-invested.
“The number of corporate suspects may increase as our investigations continue,” he said at a press conference in Pontianak, West Kalimantan, on Thursday, which was streamed live on social media.
Asep said the corporate suspects have designated management representatives for legal proceedings, with investigation papers to be submitted to public prosecutors before heading to court.
The companies are being investigated under Articles 98, 99, and 108 of the Environmental Protection and Management Law, which cover deliberate or negligent environmental offences and land burning.
The offences carry penalties of up to 15 years' imprisonment for individuals found liable and fines of up to 15 billion rupiah (RM3.36 million).
“We are proceeding against foreign-affiliated companies or those funded by overseas investment because the alleged offences occurred within the jurisdiction of the Republic of Indonesia,” he said.

Asep said police have recommended the revocation of business licences of 23 corporations following findings that included repeated fires within concessions, fires originating on company land, inadequate firefighting facilities, and burnt areas exceeding 500 hectares.

He said police had so far received 104 reports involving corporations, covering 29,168.78 hectares of burnt land, including 33 reports in West Kalimantan, 20 in South Sumatra, 14 in Central Kalimantan, 13 in South Kalimantan, and seven in East Kalimantan.
For cases involving individuals, police have filed 287 reports covering 5,859.12 hectares of burnt land, with 245 people named as suspects.
West Kalimantan recorded the highest number of police reports involving individuals, at 68, followed by Riau (59), Central Kalimantan (43), South Sumatra (42) and East Kalimantan (30).
Asep said that individual cases generally involved deliberate or negligent burning to clear land, with suspects investigated under environmental protection, plantation, and forestry laws.

6c7563d057b9fb20: TOKYO: Fast-fashion giant Uniqlo has cancelled a planned price hike for its popular socks in Japan, as consumers grow increasingly frustrated with inflation.
The company reversed its decision less than two weeks after announcing increases that led local media to suggest its reputation as a "symbol of affordability" was at risk.

The retail powerhouse said a planned jump to ¥390 (US$2.50) a pair for one popular category of basic socks was now officially off the board, instead opting to keep them at ¥290 and a bargain ¥990 for four pairs.

"As socks are an essential everyday item, in Japan we reconsidered our planned price revision and decided to continue our multi-buy offer," a spokesman for Uniqlo's parent company, Fast Retailing, said in a statement.
The company will still proceed with price increases for other selected items, including jackets and pants, from November largely because of soaring costs and a weak yen.
Japanese households are facing a spike in prices for everything from eggs to transport in a dramatic shift from deflation that plagued the nation for decades.
Many businesses that once prided themselves on low prices are now having to raise them.
The popular restaurant chain Saizeria apologised to its customers when announcing a hike this month.
Japan's core consumer prices rose 2.1% in September, and the Bank of Japan is soon expected to declare that the nation's underlying inflation has reached the 2.0% target.
Analysts have said Japanese firms are able to pass some costs onto consumers but not enough to fully cover them.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has identified fighting inflation as one of her top priorities.
e84e2d9e7b9cff7c: LETTER: Malaysia has made remarkable progress in expanding access to housing, most recently pushing past national targets by delivering more than 511,000 affordable housing units under the Twelfth Malaysia Plan.
Large-scale public housing programmes, urban upgrading efforts and investments in infrastructure have helped improve living conditions for many communities.

Yet new challenges continue to emerge such as rapid urbanisation, with the national urban population now exceeding 75 per cent, changing demographics, rising living costs and climate-related risks are reshaping what Malaysians need from housing today.

As we celebrate this Urban October under the theme "Adequate Housing for All", the question is whether that home is safe, affordable, resilient, well-connected and able to support a decent quality of life.

For Malaysia, as for the world, ensuring adequate housing is central to building inclusive, resilient and sustainable cities. Globally an estimated 2.8 billion people face some form of housing inadequacy, and close to 1.1 billion live in slums and informal settlements.
As climate change intensifies, the need for resilient housing, risk-informed planning and safer urban development becomes increasingly important.

Malaysia is increasingly integrating climate resilience into housing and urban development policies through nature-based solutions, resilient infrastructure and risk-informed planning approaches that seek to protect vulnerable communities while improving urban liveability.

Recognising these challenges, the country recently launched the National Housing Policy 2026-2035, which emphasises housing affordability, a more responsive relationship between housing supply and local demand, stronger housing data systems, integration of housing and transport planning, and the development of a more formal and regulated rental ecosystem.
The policy reflects an important shift: adequate housing is being recognised not only as a matter of construction, but also as a matter of urban liveability, inclusion and long-term resilience.
A decade after world leaders adopted the New Urban Agenda (NUA), the verdict is clear global progress if falling far behind schedule, Member States recommitted to these goals through 2036.
Malaysia's evolving housing agenda positions the country to lead by example to the NUA commitments.

Having hosted the Ninth World Urban Forum (WUF9) and taking on the Presidency of the UN-Habitat Assembly for 2025–2027, Malaysia is no longer following international frameworks, but actively shaping them.

Global goals only matter if they make a difference on your street. That is where UN-Habitat and URBANICE Malaysia focus their work, helping cities and states turn big international commitments into practical local plans.
One way is through Voluntary Local Reviews and Voluntary Subnational Reviews. These are health checks that cities and states carry out on themselves.
They measure how well they are doing on the Sustainable Development Goals, the targets the world has agreed on for ending poverty, protecting the planet and improving lives.
With UN-Habitat's support, Malaysian local authorities have used these reviews to see where they stand, plan with real evidence and bring more voices into decision-making.
URBANICE Malaysia also helps cities learn from one another.

Through the Malaysia Urban Innovation Hub, public forums and hands-on support for local councils, it connects people who are solving similar problems in different places, so a good idea in one town can take root in another.

All of this comes back to a simple point: a home needs a bus stop nearby, clean water, a safe park, jobs within reach and protection from floods, and some of the best ideas come from residents themselves.
At Malaysia Urban Forum 2026, held under the theme "The Future City I Want to Call Home", community members, young people and researchers shared practical ideas for better places to live.
The Ministry of Housing and Local Government (KPKT) is now funding three community-led pilot projects to put some of those ideas into action.
It is a reminder that people who live in a place usually know best what it needs.
SRINIVASA POPURI
Chief
UN-Habitat Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific

00c1d48db371312d: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 29 — Bersatu president Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin said the confidence and supply agreement (CSA) signed with the federal government today has nothing to do with a possible electoral pact with Pakatan Harapan (PH) for the Melaka polls, Free Malaysia Today (FMT) reported.

6d2b36ee51f782cd: TOKYO: Former world number one Naomi Osaka said she would "keep attempting" to get back to her Grand Slam-winning best after her season ended with a second-round exit in Japan on Thursday.
The four-time Grand Slam champion lost 6-3, 7-5 to Slovakian 18-year-old Mia Pohankova, ranked 144 in the world, at the Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo.
Osaka has not won a title this year and has not reached a Grand Slam final since she returned to tennis after a 15-month break following the birth of her daughter Shai in 2023.
The 29-year-old, now ranked 18 in the world, said she was "at peace" with herself and feeling good about her game.
"Obviously when I play a Slam, it's in my mind to challenge for it," she said.
"Unfortunately I haven't been in that position yet, and I'm going to keep attempting it.
"But if you're asking me how I think my tennis is, I think it's pretty good."
Osaka was appearing at the Pan Pacific Open for the first time in four years.
She came out onto the court wearing a red kimono-style gown with a long frilly train.
She said she chose the colour as a contrast to the blue crane-pattern outfit she wore in her opening match this week.
Osaka said she had more outfits lined up for the Tokyo crowd but "unfortunately" would not have a chance to wear them after exiting the tournament.
Osaka is known for grabbing headlines with her flamboyant custom-made outfits.
She channelled NBA fashion trailblazer Allen Iverson at the US Open and wore an audacious "jellyfish-inspired" outfit in Australia.
She also drew on her Japanese heritage with a kimono-inspired white dress at Wimbledon.
"There are so many things that go on in my mind, and it was just a creative outlet," she said.
"All the other sports are allowed to do that, and tennis is more subdued and restrained."
Osaka started the match with an ace, but former junior Wimbledon champion Pohankova soon turned the tables on her.
The Slovakian, who said she grew up watching Osaka, broke her opponent three times to take the first set and kept the momentum going to win the match.
Pohankova hit seven aces, and Osaka said it was "tricky to play someone that I know nothing about".
"It is a little difficult, but I also remember when I was in her position and I was playing players that I watched on TV," Osaka said.
"I guess age catches up to you eventually."
Canada's Leylah Fernandez progressed to the quarter-finals after beating number five seed Elise Mertens of Belgium 6-2, 7-6 (10/8).
1dd859d46c11fc3f: PUTRAJAYA: The federal government has insisted that it never breached its constitutional duty to provide special grants to Sabah between 1974 and 2021.

Senior federal counsel Ahmad Hanir Hambaly told the Court of Appeal that Sabah had received a substituted grant of RM26.7 million annually throughout the period, dubbed the “lost years”, pending an agreement with the state government.
"For 47 years, there was no objection or reference made by the state government for an independent assessor to determine a quantum (that both governments can agree on).
"Article 112D(1) of the Federal Constitution which mentioned negotiations between federal and state governments on special grants never fixed a deadline for a decision," he said.
The submissions were made in the federal government’s appeal against a 2025 High Court ruling in a judicial review application filed by the Sabah Law Society (SLS).
The state government is also a party to the proceedings.
The Kota Kinabalu High Court had ruled that the federal government breached its constitutional duties by failing to honour Sabah’s entitlement to a 40% share of net revenue over the lost years.
The court said that no reviews were conducted until 2022 and gave the federal government three months to conduct one to determine the quantum of the 40% entitlement for the years in question.
It further ordered that an agreement be reached within six months from Oct 17, 2025, the date the judgment was handed down.

Hanir said that if the Sabah government was dissatisfied with the annual RM26.7 million grant, which it claimed was insufficient for the state's development needs, it could have engaged an independent assessor to determine the quantum payable.
"Both governments had agreed for the sum under the previous and first review order to be paid within the said period pending an agreement.”
Sabah govt, SLS want lower court's ruling affirmed
In response, Sabah attorney-general Brenndon Keith Soh told the court that the state was entitled to the special grant of 40% share of net revenue.
He insisted that no reviews were initiated by either the federal or state government during the "lost years".
"Sabah’s receipt of RM26.7 million (during the lost years) does not displace our entitlement to the special grant due, following the required periodical review.”
Lawyer David Fung, appearing for SLS, urged the appeals court to reject the federal government's contention that the substituted grant of RM26.7 million, paid yearly over 47 years, was lawful.
"There was no review by the federal and state governments for 47 years," he said.
SLS was also represented by Jeyan Marimuttu, Janice Lim and Liew Yung Enn.
The panel chaired by Justice Azhahari Kamal Ramli said the court needed time to review the parties’ submissions and fixed case management on Nov 12 pending a decision.
Also on the panel hearing the appeal were Justices Ahmad Kamal Shahid and Amarjeet Singh.
A livestream of the proceedings was broadcast to the courts in Sabah and Putrajaya.
Former Sabah chief minister Joseph Pairin Kitingan and his brother Jeffrey, a former state deputy chief minister, also attended the hearing.
6027d0e7981f3043: Decentralized messaging platform Matrix is no longer the upstart it once was. The organization is now a serious challenger to the status quo as concerns about sovereignty and independence reach new heights.
At the organization's recent Malmo event, which grew attendance 30 percent year-on-year, the mood shifted from "yes, this is important" to "yes, we're rolling this out."

Matrix is an open standard for communication. It's a federated system, so there are no central hubs or overseas control to worry about, and it can be used for anything from messaging to voice over IP. Video is also supported.

The system is an alternative to services such as Microsoft Teams. It has become popular in the public sector as governments grow increasingly wary of relying on US tech giants for services that the Trump administration could switch off at will.

However, that increased interest and subsequent roll-outs have brought a level of scrutiny Matrix was not fully prepared for. A recent report regarding anonymous reaction to a roll-out of the technology by the European Commission took Element - the company that puts the lion share of the money into Matrix - by surprise.
One attendee at the Malmo conference observed, "First they [competitors] ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight you."
Matrix remains an open standard, however, the open source foundation behind it would certainly welcome more paying members.
"It's true that we're definitely getting more attention than we have had before," said Element CEO Matthew Hodgson.
"We are seeing Matrix ending up on the critical path of digital sovereignty as almost the poster child of the whole thing.

"I'm not sure that we necessarily do want to be the poster child," he added, "We didn't sign up to end up being ambassadors for digital sovereignty, roaming from government to government, but empirically that's where we've ended up, and yeah, that's going to attract attention from people who would rather everyone just kept in their traditional big tech systems."

This comes amid worries about the reliability of international partners, from early projects including France's Tchap messenger for the public sector and Germany's BundesMessenger through to more recent users, such as the Swedish public sector. Indeed, in one memorable demonstration during the Matrix event, messages were sent between French, Swedish, and NATO entities.

"I cannot overstate the strangeness," Hodgson added, "of having various national militaries phoning up every couple of days, saying, 'Look, we need to get on board Matrix too because we need to talk to this country and they're using Matrix, and we need to talk to that country, and they're using Matrix.'"
"It could be for defense, could be national security, could just be healthcare or education, public sector. But that is real. That is why there is a feeding frenzy."

Not that Element or Matrix is trying to build a better Teams than Teams. Patrick Alberts, Element's Chief Product Officer, said, "This is a digitally sovereign communication solution that, by and large, works like Teams in many aspects, but it's not set out to be the faster Porsche here..."

As for the reported complaints from the European Commission over Element's software implementation, Diana Gheorghe, EC head of sector for Communication and Collaboration Services, addressed them directly and described the anonymous complaints as "the natural friction of [a] high-profile rollout that we have done at scale."

Alexandru Vignide, EC service manager for Communication and Collaboration Services, who is very much at the pointy end of making the sovereign communication tools work, noted the speed of the rollout, which began with a proof of concept in Q4 2025, and hit laptops between July and September 2026.

The EC chose the Schengen Cloud Alliance (which includes OVHcloud) for hosting and, according to Vignide, "We wanted to provide a familiar experience for users." Not everyone is impressed with what is rolling out, but it's important to remember that change can be alarming, and this is still early days.

It is, however, a significant one. Gheorghe said that, as well as increasing resilience and business continuity, "We wanted to have vendor diversity. We also wanted to have data control and ownership of the platform."

Microsoft, as an example, would point to the sovereign capabilities of its system. As the Matrix conference kicked off, it announced new capabilities, including additional options for running AI, data services, and confidential workloads on customer-controlled platforms, and highlighted its sovereign partner ecosystem for customers who prefer local expertise.

However, Microsoft (and other tech giants) cannot escape concerns about who ultimately controls the data and what administrations might do with it. In 2025, a Microsoft representative memorably confirmed the US giant "cannot guarantee" data sovereignty to customers in France.

There is, however, a fly in the Matrix ointment. The platform is open source and, like so many open source projects, requires funding. Right now, Element accounts for much of the Matrix Foundation's funding. Hodgson finds this a little frustrating.

"If every government who is operationally dependent on Matrix put the smallest amount of money in the Foundation, the Foundation would have enough money to really start investing in the ecosystem and not be dependent on Element basically picking up the tab."
He acknowledged that things had improved in the last year, but said, "It's not good governance for an open standard to have one big player like Element effectively propping things up."

This isn't uncommon in the open source world, and it's a little disappointing given the ever-increasing importance placed on sovereignty in communications. Alberts commented: "There is confusion in the market that the thing somehow creates itself.

"No, it doesn't. It requires hardworking people. These hardworking people need to be paid, and that payment, in order to support government deployments going forward, ideally also comes from these governments. And some of them do a lot and do it in a great way, and that's amazing.
"But some don't." ®

5539e9df023ef152: SUNGAI PETANI, Oct 29 — Police have arrested a 35-year-old man over a viral video showing him allegedly driving recklessly in a red multi-purpose vehicle (MPV) bearing the word ‘Bomba’.
