3f40214d76a7be3b: SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 29 — No startup has ever grown so fast. In five years, Anthropic has become an AI giant valued at US$1 trillion (RM4.08 trillion), and it is now aiming for a record-breaking stock market debut.
But it faces three threats: rivals that are catching up, prices that are collapsing, and bills that keep climbing.
Anthropic spells out the risks in its Wall Street prospectus, published Monday.
The first is commoditisation: “the degree of differentiation among advanced AI models may narrow,” the company warns.

The San Francisco-based firm also says “substantially all of our revenue” comes from its AI tools. Unlike Google or Meta, it has no advertising empire to fall back on if business takes a hit, and no cloud business like Microsoft’s or SpaceX’s.
Investors have already grown nervous. In mid-August, shareholders were floating a valuation of US$2 trillion.
But quarter-on-quarter growth slowed from 145 per cent in the second quarter to 45 per cent in the third, cooling expectations to around US$1.5 trillion.
Cheap and open
So-called open AI models, which anyone can download and modify, are close behind closed models such as Claude or ChatGPT, which are available only through their owners’ paid services.
The performance of open models trails by only about four months on average, according to research institute Epoch AI.
They include Kimi K3.1 Pro from Chinese company Moonshot, which costs half as much as Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic’s current flagship.
And among paid models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, none has stayed on top for long.
Anthropic also acknowledges it is holding itself back: its safety measures “could slow our capability gains relative to competitors that do not adopt similar constraints.”
Still, the company says each new version of Claude has boosted sales. More than 80 per cent of its revenue last quarter came from models less than six months old.
Prices collapsing

When products look alike, prices fall. According to Morningstar, the price of having AI process the same amount of text, at the same level of performance, has dropped 97 per cent, from US$17 at the end of 2024 to 50 cents today.
Anthropic itself cut the price of Claude Opus by 20 per cent in September, and OpenAI cut the price of one of its flagship models by a factor of five in July.
The effect is already visible at Vercel, a developer platform that routes requests across AI models.
In August, more than half of the text it handled was processed by open models, up from 13 per cent in April.
Even so, Anthropic still captured nearly two-thirds of spending on the platform.
Even a 90 per cent price cut would not shrink total spending on AI as long as usage keeps growing at its current pace, said Malik Ahmed Khan, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Traffic transits past Anthropic’s headquarters in San Francisco, California October 27, 2026. — Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images/AFP pic
‘Triple whammy’
Anthropic’s costs, by contrast, are largely locked in. To stay ahead, each new Claude model has to be bigger than the last, trained on more data using more computing power.
Since late 2025, the company has committed to paying at least US$417 billion to rent chips and servers.
That is nearly 13 years of sales at its first-half 2026 pace, and the total could nearly double if cancellable or planned contracts are included.
These commitments are due no matter the state of its business, Anthropic warns.
The bet involves the entire industry: Google and Amazon are at once Anthropic’s shareholders, its suppliers and its resellers.

If AI turns out to be less profitable than expected, the International Monetary Fund fears a “triple whammy” from these intertwined investments: falling stock prices, debts that are harder to repay, and promised revenue that never materialises.
The independent research firm New Constructs called the listing “an unprecedented test of investor gullibility.”
To pay these bills, Anthropic is counting on money from the stock market, which is not unlimited.
SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket and AI company, raised record sums there in June, while Google and Meta, which are pouring fortunes into data centres, are also seeking fresh capital.
OpenAI, whose chief Sam Altman called a listing “ill-advised” this year, has chosen to wait until 2027, giving it time to see how Wall Street treats its big rival. — AFP

30c1e927c6551931: Google is working with NASA to develop a robotic medical assistant that could help astronauts on future deep-space missions.

Chocolate Factory's public sector VP Jim Kelly said in a Tuesday blog post that the company's latest moonshot could take its technology far beyond the lunar surface, with Google's public sector arm partnering with NASA's Human Research Program, Johnson Space Center's robotics team, and the Jet Propulsion Laboratory to develop a robot that could assist astronauts with medical tasks, cargo handling, and routine maintenance.

The robotics project builds on the Crew Medical Officer Digital Assistant (CMO-DA), an AI-powered medical decision-support system Google has been working on with NASA since last year. CMO-DA, which is powered by the Red Hat-supported open source local AI tool RamaLama, is already being evaluated on Earth-bound copies of computers used aboard the ISS. It’s designed to run AI models locally for evaluation of medical issues, which will be a key part of future space missions due to the communications lag between Earth and astronauts in deep space.

“An astronaut on a future deep space mission to Mars could face severe operational challenges—including round-trip communication latencies of up to 44 minutes, making real-time medical guidance for crew nearly impossible,” Kelly said in this week’s blog post.
Google and NASA envision the robot as an assistant to a human crew medical officer, helping with medical tasks and doing other work when bedside assistance isn't required.

“To maximize its utility for a lean crew, the robotic system is designed as a versatile 'payload' handler capable of managing cargo, logistics, and equipment,” Kelly explained. “When not needed for routine maintenance like organizing tools or securing compartments, it can pivot to medical support.”

As one example of its potential use, the Google public sector VP explained that, were someone to experience severe back pain potentially caused by kidney stones, the robot could fetch and prep an ultrasound machine, leaving the crew medical officer to interpret the scan and decide on treatment.

“The ultimate goal is to build a robotic system that can execute a variety of tasks via simple voice instructions, under the astronauts’ direct supervision and command,” Kelly said. “For instance, the robot might be directed to assist with routine health monitoring—such as capturing basic vitals or simple ultrasounds—under the strict guidance of a human crew medical officer.”
So, not a full-fledged digital medical officer as much as an extra set of hands for an overworked human doc.

As for the status of the project, it doesn't appear to have advanced too far yet. Google outlines several technologies being explored, including JPL's work adapting satellite situational-awareness tools originally used to track objects in orbit to help the robot navigate 3D spaces. The project remains at the proof-of-concept stage, with early laboratory demonstrations conducted, but Google hasn't confirmed whether a fully integrated, space-ready robot exists.

Kelly explained that Google used DeepMind's MuJoCo physics simulator to test the robot's movements, and that the system scored an initial 85 percent success rate in early lab tests involving locating and moving a medical bag – not exactly proof that it's ready to assist with medical procedures, but it's a start.

Google referred us to NASA for questions, but the space agency declined to get into specifics. The agency only told us it's working on a variety of "super intelligence" (eye roll - that's AI to those of us operating in reality) projects for its many missions, and that it's working with partners to assess them for future applications. ®
d29f179e903a044f: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond. But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business. Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments.

An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all.

Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%). Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes.

“There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here. It’s just not really useful in most companies today.”

The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business. A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms). It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says.

This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.
d54230b35402242a: Why ask a human to complete a coding test when they can just use an AI to help them? Anthropic engineering manager Felix Rieseberg says he has stopped using traditional coding interviews for his team.

"Being able to quickly define problems and find elegant solutions was a weak but useful predictor for how successful you’d be on my teams," Rieseberg explained in a blog post on Tuesday. "Small coding challenges in real code did tell us something meaningful about candidates."
No longer, he says. The coding interview is dead, as far as he's concerned.

"There’s no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both," he insisted. "Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests."

In a response posted to social media, Jaana Dogan, principal engineer at Google, said much the same. "I’m not doing a ton of coding interviews nowadays but I’d be interested to interview how people use coding agents," she wrote. "That itself gives me more signals about candidates' coding skills."

Several months ago, Google reportedly began reevaluating how it conducts coding interviews and what it looks for in candidates. And while it would be surprising if similar conversations haven't already occurred at other large technology companies where AI agents have demonstrated their coding capabilities, the rest of the tech industry appears to be moving more cautiously than the AI enthusiasts.

"We are not seeing tech companies abandon skills assessments widely across the industry—at least not yet," said Nicole Bachaud, labor economist at ZipRecruiter, in an email to The Register. "In fact, based on our October 2026 Employer Survey of 1,500 employers, we see the tech industry (Information sector specifically) is actually the most likely to test for skills, with 62.5 percent of employers requiring formal skill tests on initial applications."

Coding interviews at Microsoft, and later Google, Amazon, Facebook, and other tech giants, vary, depending on what the hiring organization aims to evaluate. They may probe technical knowledge related to a specific subject, coding ability in a particular language, general problem-solving skills, team-oriented behavior, or other skills.
Stripe's software engineer interview process, according to Educative, consists of a phone screening stage, a technical phone interview, and several further on-site interviews.

Rieseberg actually worked there and describes how founder Patrick Collison urged new hires to pay attention to things that seemed out of place. "His bet was that newcomers would spot friction and opportunities that old-timers had long stopped noticing," he said.

And Rieseberg appears to have absorbed that viewpoint based on his dismissal of experience: "Hunger beats tenure," he said, perhaps unaware that technology companies have gotten into legal trouble for jettisoning costly veteran employees so they can be replaced by hungry, less expensive young professionals.

Technical interviews are seldom just about technical mastery. There are after all many other ways that employees can add value to an organization beyond testable computer science skills. And when employees have access to AI models that can answer technical questions better than job candidates, it makes sense to look more closely at the creativity and social skills people bring to the table.

"The change at Anthropic might be reflecting a shift away from technical skills towards more human, soft skills," said Bachaud. "As AI becomes fully capable of writing code, tech employers may be pivoting away from rote technical testing and heavily toward human-centric soft skills."

She argues that while AI may be able to code well, it can't replace critical thinking. "A staggering 61.5 percent of Information employers now report that 'critical thinking' is a primary skill lacking in today's candidate pool," she said.

"I don’t think the coding interview is going to come back," said Rieseberg. "It's easy to get sentimental given how many copies of 'Algorithms and Data Structures' were bought in hopes of unlocking good jobs and a better future — or how the death of the coding interview is another milestone in software engineering reaching a new level of abstraction."
At the same time, he's not certain what will replace it.

"I’m probably not the only manager trying to figure out how to interview for people who build well with AI," Rieseberg wrote. "I haven't quite gotten there yet — but I’m scanning resumes and portfolios for little prototypes that exhibit taste, empathy, and principled thinking. If you have figured out something better, I’d love to hear how."

Bachaud sees technical evaluations changing instead of going away, noting that 70 percent of Information sector employers have switched to proctored or in-person skill assessments as a way to deter cheating with AI.

"Ultimately, tech companies aren't necessarily testing less, but the way they are testing is changing," she said. "As AI automates a lot of manual and technical components of jobs, work skills may become more universal. That could lead to an increase in job switching and turnover once economic conditions improve. In our recent survey of workers, we found that AI-related work concerns are causing a quarter of workers to start thinking about their next role. And as assessments and skills are changing, what roles are available to them might look more different than ever before." ®

Google’s consulting and incident response biz, Mandiant, later confirmed the data theft and extortion crew exploited CVE-2026-35273 as a zero-day, mostly against schools and the education sector.

By late September, however, Mandiant said ShinyHunters massively expanded its targeting, “deploying web shells on dozens of systems globally, spanning higher education, technology, IT services, healthcare, agriculture, transportation, and government.”

According to ZDI bug hunter Bobby Gould, there are actually three distinct vulnerabilities across multiple PeopleSoft components, and each should receive its own CVE identifier rather than being grouped under CVE-2026-35273.

Gould, along with TrendAI researchers Minh Giang and Lucas Miller, originally found and reported three distinct bugs to Oracle in June. “We are coordinating with Oracle to assign separate CVEs for each issue,” he said in a Tuesday blog.

The first issue is a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in the PeopleSoft Integration Gateway (PSIGW), which gives attackers a foothold in the PeopleSoft application. In June, Oracle introduced a “validateClient” method to allow PeopleSoft system administrators to restrict access to certain functionality. The SSRF bug, however, allows crims to make requests that satisfy the validation requirement to access endpoints vulnerable to RCE, Gould wrote.

“While this solution does restrict access, an attacker on any trusted host can still reach PSEMHUB,” he said, referring to PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB). “Because Oracle allows localhost by default, the PSIGW SSRF provides exactly that access.”

The second bug is an external control of file path vulnerability in PSEMHUB’s ExecuteProcessActivityCommand handler. This message handler is designed to allow remote clients to write log entries to the PeopleSoft server’s filesystem - but it doesn’t properly validate requests, which allows an attacker to write a web shell into a file path and achieve RCE.

The third vulnerability, also in PSEMHUB, is a deserialization of untrusted data flaw. An attacker can use a file-write vulnerability to plant a malicious XML file inside a PeopleSoft directory that stores environment configuration data, then wait for PSEMHUB to initialize, such as after a service or system restart. This triggers deserialization of the malicious XML file, potentially allowing the attacker to achieve RCE.
“Attackers can combine these vulnerabilities to compromise affected instances of PeopleSoft,” Gould warned.®

b8365cf2bf687c78: In the first round of the 2026 Brazilian presidential election, on Oct. 4, the politics of resentment prevailed. Frustration among those displaced from their jobs by automation and the newly self-employed – who sometimes wrongly see themselves as “entrepreneurs” – fueled the vote for the opposition of Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and favored far right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro. In the runoff on Oct. 25, however, the driving motivation shifted from resentment to fear of a return of the so-called “Bolsonarismo” to power. President Lula was reelected in a second round whose outcome could hardly have been anticipated from his lackluster first round campaign and Flávio Bolsonaro’s lead of 2.2 million votes. So what changed? First, Lula took his campaign to the streets, where it had been largely absent in the first round. And it also moved into social media, where Lula’s presence had preiviously amounted to little more than a translation of analog campaigning into digital formats. Another important factor was the fear generated by Flávio Bolsonaro’s first round lead. Until then, there had been a widespread conviction – not only among Lula and his campaign team, but throughout democratic society in general – that the president would be reelected. A change in attitudes The shock with the results of the first round, followed by fear of a far right victory, brought about a change in attitudes and a spontaneous mobilization in the streets, beginning with students in Brazil’s Rio de Janeiro state and spreading to large and medium sized cities across the country. Fear intensified as Flávio Bolsonaro increasingly revealed his resemblance to his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, now jailed for attempting a coup after losing his bid for reelection in 2022.. In the 27 state capitals and 162 other major Brazilian cities, encompassing nearly 75 million voters – close to 47% of the total – Lula’s gains were decisive, according to a survey by news and data analysis website Dado Bruto. He won in 13 of the state capitals, including São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro. In Minas Gerais, he lost in capital Belo Horizonte, although he carried the state. Overall, in the state capitals, Lula gained 2.2 million votes in the runoff, offsetting Flávio Bolsonaro’s first round advantage. Across the 189 Brazilian major cities, Lula’s vote share rose by nearly 3.5 percentage points. This result helped him make gains in every state. He reversed the first round defeat in Minas Gerais, improving his performance in the second round by more than three percentage points. Urban Brazil delivered Lula’s victory. He won in 12 states in the first round, and in 13 in the second. Consider Osasco, a major city in the state of São Paulo, whose GDP is overwhelmingly generated by the service industry, particularly finance, technology, logistics, and ecommerce. The city has nearly 729,000 inhabitants and a GDP per capita of R$ 164,000 (US$30,000). Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round in Osasco by 191,700 votes to Lula’s 182,700. In the runoff, Lula reversed the result, winning by 234,300 votes to 213,200. In many of these major cities, voters took to the streets in support of Lula. On social media, the extensive reach of the WhatsApp network “Exército do Lula” – or “Lula’s Army” –, with more than 10 million followers and managed by reelected congressman André Janones, certainly had a significant positive effect in generating additional votes for the president. The interaction between digital networks and street mobilization played a decisive, if not determining, role in his reelection. In the major cities of agribusiness strongholds, Flávio Bolsonaro won more than 70% of the runoff vote. A particularly representative municipality is Sinop, in the state of Mato Grosso, where he won the first round by 73,700 votes to Lula’s 17,500. In the runoff, Lula gained another 4,700 votes, while the Liberal Party candidate added 3,800, making little difference to the final result: 77,500 votes to 22,200, with Flávio Bolsonaro winning 77.7% of the votes. Urban-rural cleavage revived The expansion of export oriented agribusiness, particularly in Brazil’s center-west and north regions, but also in the South and the north-central and northwestern regions of Minas Gerais, has revived the urban-rural cleavage of Brazilian politics. This divide was at the heart of the most serious political and electoral conflicts of Brazil’s Second Republic, from 1945 to 1964. During that period, the troubled relationship between an executive branch elected by urban Brazil and a legislature whose majority was elected by rural Brazil produced legislative paralysis, contributing to the breakdown of democratic institutions that led to the 1964 coup. Today, although the rural economy is technologically advanced, this divide has taken the radicalized form of political polarization, destabilizing the political system and threatening the country’s governability. It generates an authoritarian impulse that materialized under Jair Bolsonaro’s administration. Jair Bolsonaro was convicted in September 2025 of attempting a coup and is serving his sentence. The prosecution and conviction of those involved in the attempted coup have dispelled neither radicalized polarization nor the authoritarian impulse. The latter resurfaced unmistakably in Flávio Bolsonaro’s refusal to accept the clean and democratic verdict of the ballot box. It was precisely this persistent coup oriented impulse that made the runoff mobilization possible, through a clearly visible interaction between digital networks and the streets. The decline in voter alienation, which brought 4.8 million electors back into the pool of valid votes, vividly expresses this reaction driven by fear of a return to Bolsonaro’s attempts to overthrow democratic institutions. Nearly 2.9 million additional voters turned out at the polls. Invalid votes fell from 3.7 million to 2.7 million, while blank ballots declined from 2.3 million to 1.4 million. Voter alienation dropped by three percentage points. The future of Lula’s fourth term This coup oriented impulse is particularly important when we consider the composition of the newly elected Brazilian Congress. A majority of those elected to Congress in the first round are sided with Flávio Bolsonaro. Beginning in 2027, President Lula’s room for maneuver in Congress will be narrower. In both the House of Deputies and the Senate, it will be possible to assemble a majority coalition, but one in which the center-right and right will carry greater weight. Members of the “Centrão”, Brazil’s parties known for their transactional politics, are inclined to align themselves with those in power by definition. In the House, the moderate right and the Centrão together would account for approximately 66% of a possible Lula’s coalition’s votes, and in the Senate, 56%. This would significantly alter the configuration of Lula’s fourth administration, which would rest on a broad democratic coalition, but not a progressive one. Lula intends to add digital mobilization to his presidential toolkit, drawing on the experience of “Lula’s Army”. The objective would be to raise Lula’s public approval ratings, thereby strengthening his ability to negotiate with and exert pressure on Congress. Anyway, the president would have to open up his administration further and become more receptive to parties outside his traditional political and partisan circles. This fourth term will mark the end of the Lula era. After this cycle, Brazilian politics will have to change, renew its leadership, and take into account the emerging generation of digital politicians. The end of this era also coincides with the departure from the political stage of the generation that resisted the military dictatorship that took power in 1964, from which three Brazilian presidents emerged: Fernando Henrique Cardoso, Lula, and Dilma Rousseff. Generational succession is inescapable. Brazil’s new generation of politicians will be more attuned to digital society. 221a04c5d881621c: Maximize value, not token usage, Amazon has told its engineers, citing concerns about rising AI costs and complexity.
Amazon made the strategy shift public on Tuesday in a note to engineering teams outlining the changing role of its software development engineers in the age of AI.

“Our most prolific engineers have demonstrated that neither the developer role nor their output is defined by the use of AI,” Amazon VP and distinguished engineer Terk Terkowitz wrote in the note. “We're now in the era of the Renaissance Developer, blending AI tools with human judgment and domain expertise to build entirely new things.”
In other words, Amazon wants its developers using AI, but burning through tokens isn't the same thing as getting useful work done.
Rather than define the developer role by how AI is used, the memo focuses on what isn't changing so fast: the need to deliver useful software and results for customers and the business.

“It is difficult to define, in a way that will stand the test of time, what good AI powered engineering practices look like,” the memo continues. “We have decided to focus on what is not changing as we evolved the SDE roles … the outcomes that matter aren’t changing, even if the inputs, tools, and techniques are changing faster than ever.”

What that means for software developers in the present moment is that AI input metrics, even if Amazon has seen some correlation with increased productivity and delivery on tokenmaxxing teams, aren’t what Amazon sees as a measurement of good use of developer time and resources.
“We are all aware of how deeply flawed these metrics are, primarily because they are disconnected from what matters,” the memo argues.

“[U]sing these metrics could, if used as a target instead of a measure, drive negative outcomes, increasing costs, and increasing complexity,” the memo continues, referring to tokenmaxxing costs and overly complex code that’s at odds with Amazon’s mission to “invent and simplify.”

An Amazon spokesperson confirmed that the memo’s intent was to discourage tokenmaxxing, pointing us to comments from AWS CEO Matt Garman from June in which he encouraged developers to measure outcomes, not token consumption, in making proper use of AI tools for software development.

Amazon also wants its developers thinking more about how AI can help “improve delivery for customers” and business units, not just trying to find a place to stick it to prove it's working for them. The memo calls out some engineering teams who’ve “become less connected to their customers and business,” and says teams that are more engaged with their products and business roles “are able to take the most advantage of AI and agentic software development,” in essence calling for more teams to take a similar approach.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing,” the memo said. “An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for.”

Amazon's take in the memo is starkly similar to what Microsoft told its own internal development teams in August, right down to stressing a focus on returns for customers and business instead of maximizing input.
"Tokenmaxxing is not what we are optimizing for," Microsoft EVP Jay Parikh told developers. "I want all of us focused on maximizing outcomes that move the needle for our customers and our business."

With that, the writing seems to be on the wall for the throw-AI-at-everything-and-see-where-it-sticks approach to integrating the tech. When two companies that large start to question whether AI token consumption is a useful measure of productivity for their thousands of software engineers, it's possible the rest of the world will soon start sipping those tokens instead of chugging them.

That, or we'll soon see even more enterprises begin to embrace the philosophy of relying on "good enough" open-weight models that can handle many tasks at a fraction of the cost of more expensive alternatives – Garman made a similar case for choosing cost-effective models based on the task back in June.
If you're a bubble, that approach looks an awful lot like a pin. ®

The Microsoft-owned code hosting biz also says it is redesigning its technical architecture (an effort discussed previously) to separate compute and storage, with the expectation that will enable 35x more throughput.

"We’re also migrating to a multi-region deployment in Azure, while continuing to serve incredible levels of traffic from developers around the world," said Jay Parikh, EVP of CoreAI, Microsoft, in a blog post provided to The Register. "We expect to complete the migration early next year. Those investments give us more room to grow. The next step is building the systems that handle the work."

Also at the its Universe event, GitHub announced general availability of Copilot Fusion, the company's model routing service that was previewed under the name HydraFusion. The idea is that allowing GitHub to route requests to different models can improve task-completion rates while reducing token consumption costs.

"Different tasks need different models," said Parikh. "Developers shouldn’t have to manage every model choice to get the right result at the right price. Copilot Fusion evaluates what a task needs across reasoning, code generation, debugging, and tool use, then chooses how to execute across one or more models. In the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Fusion Max scored within two points of Opus 5.5 Max at half the cost and 40% less time per task."

GitHub is making more bells and whistles available through its Copilot app, including Copilot Projects, for coordinating parallel work; Copilot Connectors, for simplifying how Copilot connects to MCP servers; and Copilot Automations, which are reusable agent tasks.

And in what appears to be an effort to boost Copilot usage in the workplace, GitHub is extending Copilot access to all GitHub Enterprise users without requiring any additional per-seat purchases. Customer still get billed for the tokens they use.

Microsoft's code collab biz is also expanding its suite of AI services for developers with an offering called AI Scans, which checks pull requests for vulnerabilities in languages not addressed by rule-based scanning and in code that's already merged, plus new reachability analysis tools that allow development to focus on issues that are plausibly exploitable. Another new offering is a package firewall that checks enterprise policy settings before fetching npm packages. ®

071e826394b5b671: For centuries, infrastructure has evolved alongside technology. New materials and engineering techniques enabled taller buildings, longer bridges, and larger cities. Computing and digital technologies later transformed how infrastructure was designed, monitored, and operated. Now, the pace of change is accelerating, and challenges are arriving simultaneously. Climate change is increasing pressure on water, energy, and other resources. Artificial intelligence is beginning to transform engineering and design, and its energy needs, along with aging grid infrastructure, is creating significant challenges, as well as new opportunities. In addition, geopolitical complexity is exposing vulnerabilities in global supply chains, and demand for infrastructure is rising, particularly in the developing world. The result is a fundamental challenge: How can the world build the infrastructure it needs without simply repeating the extractive, carbon- and resource-intensive model of the 20th century? In this interview, Ali Jadbabaie, JR East Professor and head of the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, says the answer will require rethinking not only how infrastructure is designed and built, but how it is financed and operated, and bringing together the many stakeholders who shape those decisions. On Oct. 28, Jadbabaie will join experts from around the world in Madrid to explore these topics at the World Infrastructure Forum, which was co-founded by MIT’s Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, UPM, the World Bank Group, and the University of Texas at Austin. Q: Infrastructure has always evolved in response to technological advances. What makes this era different? A: In the 18th century, civil engineering emerged as the civilian counterpart to military engineering, building the dams, bridges, and canals of its time. Industrialization in the 19th century brought railways and sewage systems. In the early 20th century, the focus scaled up to buildings, highways, tunnels, and metro systems, and by mid-century the infrastructure needed to support megacities and skyscrapers. Every time technology has changed, with information technologies, computing, sensing, and, more recently, digital transformation, it has changed the shape of infrastructure. It has even changed the definition of what infrastructure is. Today, we consider the power grid, semiconductor manufacturing plants, and data centers part of infrastructure, along with wireless infrastructure like cellphone towers and the infrastructure for high-speed internet, just as much a part of our critical infrastructure as roads, water systems, and power grids.  What is different now is the combination and speed of the changes we're facing. Climate change, resource constraints, and geopolitical instability are putting pressure on the way we designed infrastructure in the 20th century. At the same time, many people are moving out of poverty because of recent economic growth in the developing world. In fact, according to models, by 2028, for the first time in the history of humanity, the median human inhabitant of the planet will live off $10 a day. As more people move out of abject poverty, there will also be an increase in the demand for infrastructure. If we try to meet that demand using the same resource-intensive model we used in the 20th century, we simply won't have the resources to do it. The question then becomes: How do we use the remaining resources more efficiently? We need to find a way to provide more infrastructure while using less water, energy, and materials, and produce less carbon. This is where digital transformation and AI become potentially transformative. Faster and cheaper sensing, greater access to data, and better sensing, actuation, and control can help us make infrastructure decisions more efficiently. AI is slowly permeating the physical world, and we expect it to revolutionize the engineering design process, allowing us to explore many more possibilities, much faster and at a lower cost.  But the story of that hasn't been written yet, and the outcomes could still be very positive, depending on what we do. Q: Can you give an example of infrastructure systems becoming more interconnected in a way that changes how we build or manage them? A: The revolution in information technology and digital transformation over the past 30 years has made infrastructure systems more interconnected. You see this in cities. If the power goes out, water and gas systems can stop functioning, internet fails, and transportation system comes to a halt. If communications networks fail, many other services are affected. We saw this during Covid, when disruptions in supply chains affected energy networks, critical materials, and manufacturing. We see it when geopolitical conflicts disrupt oil and energy markets and those disruptions propagate through other parts of the global economy. Infrastructure systems that were once managed separately are increasingly dependent on one another. As we connect more things together for more efficiency, we also increase systemic risk and expose the systems to rare but catastrophic failures. They have become rare, but when they happen, they're much bigger and more consequential. The really tricky thing is that developing infrastructure involves much more than designing and building it. The whole value chain includes financing and operating it, as well as understanding who will use it and what those users need and prefer. So, designing infrastructure is a highly transdisciplinary, sociotechnical endeavor, involving social, technical, and economic considerations. Understanding how these systems are designed is increasingly important because they are becoming more complex, making decision-making particularly difficult. There’s also so much uncertainty in large infrastructure projects. They’re very capital-intensive, the business is lower margin than many other industries, and projects take a long time. Combine all of that, and it has historically made the industry very conservative. But the transformations coming from AI and digital transformation are potentially offering a new way forward. What that new way looks like, no one has quite delineated it yet. Q: How are you and your colleagues working to change how these decisions get made?   A: We realized that if we're going to develop a new approach to infrastructure, no single discipline, company, or country can do it alone. Infrastructure value chain is too interconnected, and the challenges are too large. That's why MIT’s Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering co-founded the World Infrastructure Forum with the World Bank Group, the Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, and University of Texas at Austin. The goal is to bring together academia, industry, governments, and financial institutions across the infrastructure value chain and create an ongoing dialogue about how infrastructure should be designed, financed, built, and operated in the decades ahead. This is particularly important because the biggest opportunities for new infrastructure development are not necessarily in the United States or other countries with mature infrastructure systems. Those countries still face significant needs for modernization and new investment. But over the coming decades, much of the world's population growth, and much of the infrastructure that will need to be built, will be in countries where infrastructure systems are still developing.  Those countries have an opportunity to benefit from modern infrastructure without simply repeating the model of the 20th century. But capturing that opportunity will require new approaches to technology, financing, engineering, and governance. We're trying to create an ecosystem rather than just a forum, a mechanism for continuing the conversation among the different stakeholders across the infrastructure value chain. We've established five working groups and an advisory group of more than 30 leaders from across the infrastructure value chain, including engineering and construction, materials, finance, multilateral institutions, and academia. Ultimately, the question is not whether we need a new way of developing infrastructure. The question is how we create it and who is going to execute it. There is no single person, company, or country that can solve this problem, because infrastructure itself is interconnected. We need to build the new model together.
ee0f6bebf043544c: Ukrainian ransomware crook Artem Stryzhak has been sentenced to 70 months in the slammer by a New York federal court for his role as an affiliate of the Nefilim and Hive ransomware gangs.
Prosecutors believe the cybercriminal began working with Nefilim in or around June 2021, while living in Barcelona, Spain.

The Nefilim ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation was known for targeting wealthy companies, with its operators encouraging affiliates to pursue businesses capable of paying substantial ransom demands.
One of Nefilim's most high-profile attacks was on Australian logistics giant Toll Group in 2020, encrypting its files roughly three months after it suffered a separate Mailto ransomware attack.
Court documents [PDF] state that Stryzhak agreed with alleged Nefilim boss Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, who remains at large, to pay the ransomware crew a 20 percent cut of the ransom proceeds he collected.

Tymoshchuk told Stryzhak that his preference was for attacks to target companies based in the US, Canada, and Australia that turn over more than $100 million annually. This guidance was soon tweaked to encourage targeting companies in the same regions with more than $200 million in annual revenue.

Prosecutors claim that around the time Stryzhak joined forces with Nefilim, he also signed up to the Hive ransomware operation as "one of its earliest affiliates," and used its platform to attack approximately seven victims. Hive's operators claimed they targeted circa 1,500 victims worldwide between June 2021 and January 2023.

According to separate court documents [PDF], Hive's victims included a law firm and an Ohio hospital, which paid approximately $1.7 million in Bitcoin after the gang initially demanded $2 million during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Before its infrastructure was seized in an international law enforcement operation in January 2023, Hive was known for attacking healthcare facilities during the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as being one of the ransomware groups that battered Costa Rica in 2022.

Brett Leatherman, assistant director at the FBI’s cyber branch, described Stryzhak as a “prolific cybercriminal” who played a role in groups that were responsible for more than $100 million in victim damages.
“Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak’s crimes and demonstrates the FBI’s global reach and extensive network of international partners,” he said.

“Multiple field offices contributed to this investigation, and our work does not end here. We will continue to leverage every tool at our disposal to track down Stryzhak’s co-conspirators and hold them accountable, including Volodymyr Viktorovych Tymoshchuk.”
Stryzhak was arrested by Spanish police in June 2024 before being extradited to the US in April 2025.

In announcing Stryzhak's sentencing, the Justice Department took the opportunity to remind the public that rewards totaling up to $11 million are available for qualifying information about alleged Nefilim operator Volodymyr Tymoshchuk and other key ransomware suspects. ®

133598f3f99fbe16: Donate to our Justice as infrastructure Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!

All images via Canva or fair use. Screenshots of Peacekeeping circle (bottom left) and Duterte protest (top center) via YouTube. International Criminal Court building (top right) via Wikimedia CC BY-SA 4.0. St. Louis courthouse under construction (center middle) via Picryl CC0 1.0.

Often portrayed as abstract, large, formal, distant, and quite technical, justice is a moral and ethical area, tied to institutions and legal statutes, and can seem a long way from mundane daily experience. But it is also a deeply practical underpinning for how most societies function. Without justice systems that work and are understood at the most fundamental level, economic mobility is threatened, socially marginalized groups have no recourse, and lack of trust hampers institutions and interpersonal interactions alike.

Justice is the grease in the motor of social functioning. Nobody will contest the importance of justice to holding people to a collective moral code of conduct, but the often overlooked next-level function justice plays is that, when justice is fair, fast, and reliable, it makes everything in a society run better. It allows for a society to fulfill its economic, social, and creative potential. Copyright law protects ideas and innovation; land law protects resources and livelihoods; labor law supports humane and effective use of our work — as long as those laws are enforced. When you know that it will be straightforward and predictable to get all the permits, you are more likely to start a business. When you know that fraud will be punished, you are more likely to invest your capital. When you know that you will be caught, you’re less likely to evade taxes. When you know that there will be fair and fast prosecution, you are more likely to report injustice and less likely to perpetrate it.

In this spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to make visible the ways in which justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society, and how countries with a justice deficit can work towards stronger protections that will enable economic and social benefits.

33c673a8d5cb4cdb: A cartoon from an ex-Google software engineer, titled “Welcome to Google,” made the rounds a while back. It featured two diverging roads, neither passable. One was the main road, marked as deprecated (“don’t even think about it,” the sign read). The new road, however, was marked as still under construction (“Danger”), and so was unusable as well.

That was the no-win choice two million frontend developers faced in 2014, when Google unexpectedly deprecated its popular JavaScript framework, AngularJS, in favor of Angular 2, which had a radically different architecture, a confusing name, no upgrade path, and wasn’t even fully released yet.
So, many developers turned the wheel and headed to Reactville or Vuetown instead.

How Google botched the Angular upgrade provides timely lessons in how not to update a software package, which former Google Developer Advocate Stephen Fluin outlined in a talk at the All Things Open conference last week.
“Uncertainty kills motivation,” said Fluin. “When you're taking away everything [developers] know and love, they're going to feel disheartened.”
Fluin is now head of developer relations for Buildkite, but he worked for Google from 2016 to 2021 on the Angular project.

“Things were a little bit rough at the time. It was a bit of a death march,” he told the audience. “We had no idea when Angular 2 was going to come out, and the core fundamentals of Angular kept changing.”
From AngularJS to Angular 2
Google had good reasons for updating Angular.

The AngularJS team had been snatched from Google’s infrastructure division and placed under its ad division, where the software could be more fully exploited. To support operations of that size, Angular needed greater rigor.

The original AngularJS was launched in 2009 as a side project of Google engineer Miško Hevery, who wanted to extend HTML. Google pulled AngularJS into an internal project because Google developers found it easier to work with than the Java-based Google Web Toolkit (GWT).
The framework quickly caught on with outside web developers too, who readily understood the angle brackets of HTML (hence the name) and wanted more interactive components.
Hevery built AngularJS 1.3 with a traditional controller model, which handled all user input, logic and data transport under the JavaScript $scope object.

Angular 2, announced at the ng-europe 2014 conference, was a major shift in architecture. It shifted to a component model, with each HTML template enjoying its own class properties. After a forced, unhappy dalliance with Google's Dart, the team rewrote Angular completely in TypeScript, with no backward compatibility whatsoever.

It was a lot to take in, and the introductory talk at ng-europe seemed to spook Angular developers more than inspire them. For each discarded feature, the speakers displayed a graphic of a tombstone (“RIP Controllers”) and played a recording of a church bell tolling in the background.
“That talk is still infamous today for what it did to the community,” Fluin said. “All these things that you know and love about AngularJS are gone. They're dead. And nobody knew this was coming.”

In general, it was not a good time for software migrations, Fluin noted in his talk. Python was having a rough time migrating from version 2 to 3, as was the KDE desktop moving from version 4 to version 5. And the rocky transition from GNOME 2 to 3 still loomed in the rearview mirror for many.
What's in a name?
“If you're trying to bring your developers with you, give them a path. Don't just kill your old thing and then not have a new thing ready,” Fluin advised.
Many devs defected to React and Vue.js, two other JavaScript frontend frameworks that also embraced the component model and were already in production.

In the 2016 State of JS Survey, React was the most popular frontend framework, with 53 percent of JS devs reporting that they had used it. Angular’s audience was heavily bifurcated; 30 percent still used the classic version while only 13 percent used Angular 2. Ten percent of users adopted the still up-and-coming Vue.

Angular 2 was finally released in September 2016, followed by Angular 4 the following March. Version 3 was skipped entirely for no discernable reason. Meanwhile, AngularJS classic, which was not formally retired until the end of 2021, was updated to version 1.5 in the spring of 2016, introducing components.

Muddying the waters further was the naming of the frameworks, which confounded many casual observers. Was AngularJS different from Angular 2? And was the “2” part of the Angular name, signaling the complete architectural shift, or its version number?

Getting the public to understand the name change turned out to be a major quagmire. Fluin said: “We had to fix public communication guidelines. We had to train experts. We had to fix Google's knowledge graph,” which is Google’s database of facts about the world.
“Naming and versioning matter,” he told the audience. “They don't matter in a pure technical sense, but they matter to human beings because it's human beings you're trying to keep up to date with.”

It would be easy to blame the Google brass for nearly shipwrecking Angular, but it has been a success at meeting Google’s needs. Today, the component-driven Angular powers Gemini’s user interface, Google Analytics, and countless other Google apps. It is now converging with Google’s internal Wiz high-performance framework, originally designed for the ill-fated Google+ social network.

Angular has also settled into a more predictable and user-friendly update pattern. Updates have a routine release cadence, currently twice a year. They dutifully follow semantic versioning guidelines, with major version numbers signifying breaking changes. Google tests each new version of the framework on its own apps before releasing it publicly. Any feature slated for removal is deprecated for a year first.
But in retrospect, Google may have been better off giving Angular 2 an entirely different name, even if it meant building up a new user base from scratch.
“JavaScript developers loved trying new frameworks. So, pretending to be a new framework might have been better,” Fluin told The Register. ®

fdc9c053616efe5d: You've probably heard, at this point, about the big changes coming to Meta's AI scraping terms for business accounts. Nieman Lab had that scoop, and since then, small businesses, journalists, and artists using Meta products like Instagram have been raising the alarm. But if you're in the EU or UK, you might be in luck and can object to that use of your data, as some users have pointed out.
If You're In the UK or EU, Here's How to Object to Meta's AI Training

Earlier this month, Meta updated its commercial terms of use for business accounts to allow it to “use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta’s products.

Many artists and small business owners that rely on Instagram and Facebook are livid at Meta granting itself permission to use their content, including from websites simply connected to their Meta accounts, to train AI. But for users in the United Kingdom and European Union, for now, there’s a way to object.

Meta buried this change in its Commercial Terms, and Nieman Lab first reported on the change. The update was originally set to go into effect on October 30, but following backlash, Meta changed the effective date to November 20. Adding to the confusion, Meta then removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases, Nieman Lab reported, and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” where previously it said that data would be used for all Meta products. Those terms still allow Meta plenty of leeway for scraping users’ data to develop its products, however.

Several users based in the UK and EU have explained how to object on Instagram. On mobile: by clicking the three lines on their account, going to the privacy center, and clicking “object,” which goes to a form that asks users to write why they are objecting to their data being used. They received an email from Meta saying their objections were approved.

The update was originally set to go into effect on October 30, but following backlash, Meta changed the effective date to November 20. Adding to the confusion, Meta then removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases, Nieman Lab reported, and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” where previously it said that data would be used for all Meta products. Those terms still allow Meta plenty of leeway for scraping users’ data to develop its products, however.

EU users’ personal data rights are governed by the General Data Protection Regulation and the AI Act. GDPR, which became enforceable in 2018, requires explicit consent to use personal data. This includes the right to object to one’s data being used. The AI Act, which went into effect in 2024, dictates how AI companies can use personal data, and how people can opt in or out, stating that they can withdraw consent at any time. The UK has its own version of the GDPR. The European Commission states: “The GDPR rules only apply to personal data about individuals; they do not govern data about companies or any other legal entities. However, information in relation to companies may constitute personal data where it allows the identification of a natural person.”

Several users based in the UK and EU have explained how to object on Instagram. Instagram user bookish.sil posted a walkthrough of how they did it on mobile: by clicking the three lines on their account, going to the privacy center, and clicking “object,” which goes to a form that asks users to write why they are objecting to their data being used. They received an email from Meta saying their objection was approved. Instagram user jenniqueart posted a similar walkthrough with the same results.

My Meta accounts are based in the US, but using a VPN to locate my IP address in London, I could see options in my Meta privacy settings that would let me object to the use of my information by Meta AI. To get there on desktop with a VPN on, I went to my account privacy center, clicked “Submit a privacy rights request” at the bottom, selected Instagram, clicked “How can I object to the processing of my information?” and got to a page where I could choose to object to the use of my information for Meta AI or third parties, which were two separate options.
When my location is based in the US, these options don't appear.

When I clicked through the option to “object to the use of my information for Meta AI,” however, it returned an error page that said “This form is only available to people in certain regions.” GDPR is meant to apply to wherever someone is located at the time, but since this objection applies to the preferences of one account, it might be based on where the account was created. I tried again located in Belgium and got the same results. I’ve asked Meta to clarify.

As many have already pointed out in the comments on UK and EU users who’ve posted walkthroughs, these objection steps aren’t available to people outside of those countries, and as Meta continuously changes its platform, these steps might not work for everyone always. Unless something changes before November 20, the rest of us are screwed.
6b3a7de94c538112: Trillium Asset Management wants Microsoft to explain how it will meet its 2030 greenhouse gas (GHG) emission targets, and is backing a shareholder proposal to request this information at the firm’s next shareholder meeting.

The cloud and software biz set itself lofty environmental goals back in 2020, aiming to be become "carbon-negative" by 2030, and to have removed the equivalent of all the carbon it has ever emitted by 2050.

But since the start of the decade, an explosion in AI development and demand for ever more complex models has seen a boom in demand for high-performance compute infrastructure and a construction wave to deliver new datacenters to house it all in.
Microsoft is one of the firms to profit from this huge demand, with its cloud division making $214.4 billion in revenue for the fiscal year 2026 ended June 30, a 27 percent year-on-year increase.

This has also caused Microsoft’s emissions to head in the wrong direction, with figures from the company’s most recent Environmental Sustainability Report showing that these have increased from 13 million tons of CO2 equivalent in 2020 to 20 million tons in 2025.
However, Microsoft estimates that without the carbon reduction initiatives it has already put in place, emissions would now be much higher, somewhere near 34 million tons.

The increase is largely accounted for by indirect emissions (Scope 3) from the construction and provisioning of datacenters to meet that demand for cloud services and AI training. But as The Register pointed out, 2025 saw a growing contribution from Scope 2, due to generation of energy the company purchased. This represents 13 percent of total emissions – up from 2 percent in 2024.

Now Trillium Asset Management, financial advisors specializing in sustainable and responsible investing, is urging Microsoft shareholders to vote for Proposal 4 during their annual meeting scheduled for December 8.

In an SEC filing, the proposal asks Microsoft to disclose additional information illustrating how it will manage climate commitments. This disclosure should go beyond existing disclosures, at reasonable cost, omitting proprietary information, and be made annually.

The proposal notes that when Microsoft first announced its carbon negative goal, it said progress required "not just a bold goal but a detailed plan," and that transparency was one of the guiding principles for this climate plan.

It states that emissions are now 62 percent above the 2020 baseline, and simply asks Microsoft to apply the principles it articulated in 2020; show the plan, be candid about the math, and explain how it will adapt.

In the filing, Trillium warns that falling short of its climate targets may create risk to Microsoft’s credibility, which can influence investor trust. If Microsoft is in danger of failing to meet its 2030 commitments, it could suffer reputational harm, and the filing claims it is already the subject of legal action by investors alleging insufficient disclosure of its AI and cloud spending.

On the flip side, it says that disclosure of a climate transition plan will likely prove valuable to large institutional investors who view climate change as a systemic risk to future economic growth.

We asked Microsoft for comment, but it already recommended in another SEC filing that shareholders vote against the proposal, arguing it fails to show that Microsoft’s existing disclosures are insufficient for investors to assess its climate-related strategy and performance.

Instead, the firm says that the proposal requests a collection of new disclosures that go beyond not just legal and regulatory requirements, but also established voluntary climate-reporting frameworks.

The proposal seeks hypothetical scenarios, contingency plans and other forward-looking information that is inherently uncertain and subject to change, Microsoft states, saying it will remain focused on its Sustainability Report and other environmental reporting while meeting any new disclosure mandates that may arise globally. ®

c11769620a3fa457: Security is the dominant feature of the EU's new Arctic strategy. dotshock / ShutterstockThe EU recently presented its latest Arctic strategy. It is the bloc’s fifth such strategy since 2008 and the first to be published since 2021, a few months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. This conflict has disrupted Arctic governance. The work of the Arctic Council, which includes Russia as one of its eight member states, was paused shortly after the invasion. The council is the primary forum for cooperation in the region. Since 2022, the Russian security threat in the Arctic has also grown. Russia has engaged in hybrid activities in the region, ranging from disinformation operations and GPS jamming to the targeting of pipelines and undersea cables. The EU’s new strategy has four priorities: strengthening peace, security and resilience in the Arctic, addressing climate change, delivering economic development and ensuring regional and social development for Arctic communities. These priorities are broadly in line with the previous 2021 strategy, in which geopolitical issues were already more present than in earlier years. But there are several major changes. More security and less climate action A word count reveals the profound impact the deteriorating cooperation context has had on the EU’s stance on the region. In the latest update, the word “security” is mentioned 52 times compared with 23 times in 2021. By contrast, “climate change” appears only 14 times in the new strategy compared with 30 times previously. This shift towards security is a general trend in the Arctic since 2022. The creation of an annual Arctic Security Conference in 2024, which discusses security trends in the region, is an example of this. Security also figures prominently in recently published national Arctic strategies, including France, Italy, Germany and Sweden. Climate change is not completely absent from the EU’s latest Arctic strategy, and the bloc reaffirmed its commitment to combat it in the document. But, where previously climate change was the cornerstone of the EU’s Arctic engagement, it is now presented through a security lens. Climate change is identified as “amplifying security risks” and a “defining threat” from which Arctic inhabitants need to be “protected”. Security shapes all four priorities of the new strategy. Arctic communities also get much more attention than in earlier documents. Although the inclusion of Indigenous people also figures more prominently, the conflation between Indigenous and local people has previously been criticised by the Saami Council. The conflation undermines the specific rights and distinct interests of Indigenous groups such as the Sámi. A ‘northern neighbourhood’ Another key change in the EU’s new Arctic strategy is the introduction of the concept of a “northern neighbourhood”. The name suggests similarities with the EU’s European Neighbourhood Policy, which it launched in 2004 to foster closer ties with its eastern and southern neighbours. But it is unclear what exact form the northern neighbourhood will take. The northern neighbourhood is not presented as a new multilateral institution. Instead, it has been put forward as a political framework enabling cooperation projects and integration between the EU and “like-minded” partners such as Greenland, Norway, Iceland, Canada and the UK. By excluding Russia, this new political framework signals a change in the EU’s understanding of the Arctic. The EU’s early engagement in the region came from a will to extend European integration to the east and north in the 2000s. The Arctic was also an area where cooperation with Russia was possible, despite disagreements elsewhere. The concept of a northern neighbourhood reveals a geographical shift in focus towards Greenland and the west and north Atlantic more generally. Yet while the US is still listed among the potential members of the northern neighbourhood, it comes with implicit conditions. According to the new strategy, a partnership with the US needs to be “predictable” and based on “shared interests and values”. This is reminiscent of the language that prevailed for Russia in the previous policies. What kind of power is the EU? Perhaps the biggest change in the new strategy lies in the document’s affirmation that multilateral cooperation “can no longer be the sole foundation of the EU’s Arctic approach”. This means two things. First, that multilateralism is no longer the prominent form of cooperation in the Arctic. And second, that the EU’s geopolitical stance in general is changing from being the champion and embodiment of multilateralism to another form of power. This is also visible in the emphasis the new strategy puts on the EU’s material capabilities and infrastructures as conditions for security. It includes mention of, among other things, developing Europe’s capacity to build icebreaker vessels. The EU’s new Arctic strategy signals a broad shift in the European geopolitical mindset. Climate change and multilateralism have been overshadowed by security concerns due to the fractured Arctic geopolitical landscape. However, ultimately, climate change and social concerns will remain key priorities of Arctic inhabitants and the EU should not lose sight of this. Emilie Canova does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
ca0f5a1a0dc47e76: The rapid decline of Antarctic sea ice since 2016 has triggered a dramatic shift in a crucial part of Earth’s climate system, scientists say.

In a paper published Wednesday, researchers documented a sharp salinity increase in a vast layer of the Southern Ocean, extending from 2,300 to 4,000 feet deep and encircling Antarctica. The shift reverses decades of freshening and echoes ocean changes usually associated with major global climate shifts over millennia but is now happening in just a few years.

The switch from a decades-long trend of freshening water to increasing salinity has implications that could extend beyond Antarctica. The layer, known as Antarctic Intermediate Water, spreads northward into the Indian, Pacific, and Atlantic oceans, transporting heat, carbon, oxygen, and nutrients toward the tropics, and even across the equator, said co-author Bishakhdatta Gayen, a researcher and professor at the University of Melbourne and at the Centre for Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences in Bengaluru, India.
1cfcc1074a1e8e54: China's secretive spaceplane has been spotted in orbit by a US commercial satellite, according to the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA)

The DIA's report [PDF] warns of developments by China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea that allegedly threaten space security, at least from a US perspective. Most of the report details systems still under development, but one image on page 53 stands out: China's spaceplane, snapped in orbit in 2024 by Maxar Technologies.

The image has been seen before; a low-resolution snap from an industry symposium was shared by Bluesky user @dutchspace almost two years ago. However, the higher-resolution image in the DIA report shows more detail. The spaceplane also bears a distinct resemblance to the US Space Force's X-37B.

The uncrewed X-37 began as a NASA project in 1999 before the US Department of Defense took over. After several atmospheric tests with an X-37A variant, the X-37B was launched in 2010. The reusable spaceplane can spend years in orbit, conducting classified activities. So far, it has launched eight times.

According to the DIA's report, China's first spaceplane mission launched in 2020 and remained in orbit for two days. A second, launched in 2022, spent 276 days in orbit, and a third, launched in December 2023, spent 268 days in oribt. The last two missions appeared to include approach and rendezvous tests of objects in orbit.

Russia, memorably, had a spaceplane in the ill-fated Buran, which bore an uncanny resemblance to the US Space Shuttle (although the two were very different beasts from a technical perspective – not least, Buran's orbiter did not carry the engines used to launch it to space).
However, according to the DIA's report, Russia "has made little progress since."
The US recently confirmed that it has weapons in space, and it would be naive not to assume rivals would have their own, whether kinetic or some form of jamming technology.

Earlier this month, Russia's Kosmos-2612 sidled up to the US ICEYE-X36 satellite before retreating. It's unclear whether the intention was an entirely innocent look at a fellow spacecraft or a bit of saber-rattling; it certainly worried US lawmakers. ®
